basic_skills.name: Temporal Gaze
basic_skills.description: Vikram's third eye glows, and he focuses on a target. He sees their past, present, and future—their sins, their virtues, their death. The target feels exposed, judged, and momentarily paralyzed by the weight of being truly seen.

basic_skills.name: Trishul Thrust
basic_skills.description: He thrusts his trident forward, and a beam of blue light shoots forth, piercing through any illusion, shield, or defense. The attack deals true damage that cannot be blocked.

basic_skills.name: Damaru Beat
basic_skills.description: He shakes his damaru once, and a pulse of sound expands outward. Allies feel their spirits lifted, their courage strengthened. Enemies are momentarily disoriented, their spells disrupted.

passive_skill.name: Presence of Time
passive_skill.description: Vikram's mere presence slows time around him. Within his vicinity, enemies move slower, their attacks delayed, their reactions dulled. Allies feel as if they have more time to act, their movements slightly accelerated. The effect intensifies the longer he remains in one place, as if time itself is reluctant to pass.

special_skills.name: Judgment of the Third Eye
special_skills.description: His third eye blazes with golden light, and he focuses on a single target. For a moment, they experience their entire life simultaneously—every joy, every sorrow, every sin, every virtue. The weight of this revelation can stun them, break them, or, in rare cases, enlighten them. The judgment is absolute and cannot be appealed.

special_skills.name: Karma Kharga Slash
special_skills.description: He swings his curved sword in a wide arc. The blade does not cut flesh—it cuts through karmic bonds, freeing allies from curses, negative effects, and spiritual bondage. Enemies find their protections stripped away, their illusions shattered.

special_skills.name: Kaal Kapala Revelation
special_skills.description: He raises his skull cup, and from it pours the light of time itself. The light washes over the battlefield, revealing all hidden things—invisible enemies, concealed traps, secret doors, and the true nature of every being present. Nothing can hide from the light of time.

special_skills.name: Trishul of Eternity
special_skills.description: He plants his trident and channels his power. The three prongs blaze with blue, gold, and white light, and from them, three beams shoot forth—one into the past, one into the present, one into the future. The target is struck simultaneously in all three times, taking damage that cannot be healed because it has already happened and will happen.

ultimate_skill.name: Mask-Bound Mortal's Judgment: The Face of Eternity
ultimate_skill.description: Vikram's mask blazes with absolute darkness and golden light, the third eye opening wider than should be possible, the flame mane around his face igniting with actual fire—black fire that does not burn but consumes time itself. He raises all four weapons simultaneously—the trident piercing upward, the damaru shaking with the rhythm of creation, the kharga swinging in an arc of judgment, the kapala pouring forth the light of all moments at once. For a single, eternal moment, time stops. Not slows—stops completely. Everything freezes: enemies mid-attack, allies mid-cheer, even the dust motes in the air. And in that frozen moment, Vikram walks among them. He looks at each enemy, truly looks, with his third eye blazing, and he sees them—all of them, every life they have lived, every death they will die, every soul they have touched. He does not judge them with anger or hate; he simply witnesses. And in that witnessing, they are revealed—to themselves, to each other, to the universe. When time resumes, the battle is over. Not because anyone is dead, but because everyone has seen the truth of themselves and cannot continue. Enemies lay down their weapons, weeping or enlightened. Allies stand in awe, forever changed. And Vikram, the mortal who wore eternity, simply turns and walks away, his sandals clicking softly on the stone, his skulls rattling gently, his mask facing forward, forever unreadable. He has done what he was made to do. He has witnessed. He has judged. He has reminded them all that time is watching, and time, unlike Vikram, never forgets.

tragedy.loss: He has forgotten his own face. Centuries of wearing the mask have erased the memory of what he looked like, who he was, the man named Vikram. He exists now only as Bhairav, a god's face on a mortal's body, a servant who became a symbol and in doing so, lost himself.
tragedy.hope: Sometimes, late at night, he stands before the temple where he once worked, and he watches the new keeper tend the masks. He watches them clean the face of Kaal Bhairav—a new mask, a replica, for the original is on his face—and he feels, for a moment, a flicker of his old self. The memory fades quickly, but it comes. It always comes. As long as someone tends the masks, as long as the temple stands, as long as there is someone who remembers the keeper, Vikram is not entirely gone.

title: The White Elephant of Perfect Memory
nickname: Gajendra Mukuta Dhari, He Who Remembers Every Prayer
lore: In the beginning, when the Kathmandu Valley was still a primordial lake, the gods descended to create a home for humanity. Indra brought thunder, Varuna brought waters, and Agni brought fire. But it was Ganeśa, the elephant-headed remover of obstacles, who brought wisdom. As he blessed the valley, a single tear fell from his eye—a tear of pure compassion for the mortals who would struggle and suffer in the world below. Where that tear landed, a white lotus bloomed, and from that lotus emerged the first Pulunkisi—a divine white elephant, radiant as the morning sun, whose very presence could dispel ignorance and illuminate truth. This elephant, named Gajendra Smritidhwaj, became the guardian of the valley's collective memory, the keeper of every prayer, every hope, every dream ever whispered by human lips. For millennia, Gajendra wandered the valley unseen, visible only to those pure of heart. He would appear to children in moments of fear, to lovers in moments of doubt, to the dying in moments of transition, offering wisdom and comfort. But as the ages passed and humanity grew more complex, more divided, more forgetful, Gajendra realized that he could not be everywhere at once. The prayers were too many, the suffering too vast, the need too great. He needed a human vessel, a mortal who could carry his power and become his eyes and ears among the people. He chose the Maharjan caste—farmers and gardeners, tillers of the very soil that had once been the primordial lake. They were humble, connected to the earth, untouched by the pride of kings or the greed of merchants. To them, Gajendra gifted a mask—not a face to hide behind, but a face to become. The mask was carved from the tusk of the first Pulunkisi himself, white as moonlight, intricate as a cosmos, embedded with patterns that told the story of creation. Only those born of the Maharjan bloodline could wear it; for anyone else, the mask would be simply wood and paint. But for a Maharjan, it was a doorway to divinity. For generations, the mask passed from father to son, from mother to daughter, always to the one whose heart was purest, whose compassion was deepest, whose connection to the people was strongest. Each bearer became Surtel—a title meaning 'He Who Carries the Light'—and each bore the weight of every prayer, every hope, every tear of the valley. They lived ordinary lives among ordinary people, farming the fields, tending the gardens, laughing at festivals and weeping at funerals. But when they donned the mask, they became something more: the living memory of the valley, the divine elephant made flesh, the remover of obstacles and the giver of wisdom. Surtel Kahalman Maharjan was born on the night of the fullest moon, under skies so clear that the stars seemed to reach down and touch the earth. From infancy, he was different—not in the way of power or precociousness, but in the way of stillness. While other children played and shouted, Surtel would sit quietly, watching, listening, absorbing. He seemed to understand things before they were explained, to know things before they were told. His grandmother, the eldest of the Maharjan, recognized the signs. She began training him in secret, teaching him the old ways, the hidden histories, the sacred responsibilities that would one day be his. When he was sixteen, the previous bearer—his own father—died peacefully in his sleep, the mask resting on his chest. That night, Surtel had a dream. Gajendra Smritidhwaj appeared to him, not as an elephant but as a being of pure light, and spoke: 'You will carry my face, my son. You will remember what others forget. You will hold every prayer ever whispered in this valley. You will feel every hope, every fear, every joy and sorrow of every soul who calls this place home. It will be beautiful beyond measure. It will be crushing beyond endurance. Are you willing?' Surtel awoke with tears on his cheeks and answered aloud to the empty room: 'I am willing.' The moment he first donned the mask, the world exploded into light. He saw everything—every prayer ever offered in the valley, from the first humans who worshipped the sun to the last breath of his own father. He felt every hope, every fear, every desperate wish, every quiet moment of gratitude. He heard the whispers of children asking for protection, the cries of mothers begging for their sick babies, the silent pleas of old men facing death alone. For three days and three nights, he lay motionless, his body overwhelmed, his mind expanding to contain the impossible. On the fourth day, he rose. He was no longer just Surtel Kahalman Maharjan. He was Surtel Kahalman Maharjan, bearer of the Pulunkisi mask, keeper of the valley's memory, the white elephant made flesh. For twenty years now, he has carried this burden and this blessing. By day, he works the fields like any other Maharjan, his handsome face known to all, his gentle smile a comfort to those who meet him. By night, when prayers grow desperate and hope runs thin, he dons the mask and walks the streets of Kathmandu. He appears to the grieving, the frightened, the lost. He speaks wisdom gathered from a million souls. He touches brows and lifts burdens. He remembers every prayer ever offered, and in remembering, he honors the faith of every being who has ever called this valley home. But the mask does not only give; it also takes. Surtel carries the weight of every unanswered prayer, every hope that died, every faith that faltered. He knows the names of those who prayed and were not saved, the faces of children who begged and still suffered, the desperate cries that faded into silence. This weight would crush any ordinary soul, but Surtel has learned to transform it—to let it become compassion rather than despair, to let it fuel his dedication rather than extinguish it. He is not a god; he cannot answer every prayer. But he can remember them, and in remembering, he ensures that no hope is ever truly lost. Now, as ancient forces stir and the valley faces threats it has not seen in millennia, Surtel feels a new weight gathering. The prayers have changed—they speak of darkness approaching, of old evils awakening, of a need for protection beyond the ordinary. He knows that soon, he may have to do more than remember. He may have to act. The mask of the white elephant is not a weapon, but wisdom can be a weapon. Memory can be a shield. And the collective hope of a million souls, channeled through one who loves them, can move mountains. He is Surtel Kahalman Maharjan, and he is ready—not for battle, but for whatever comes. He will remember. He will witness. He will, if necessary, stand.
description: Surtel Kahalman Maharjan is a vision of divine masculinity and mortal humility combined—a man so impossibly handsome that artists have wept trying to capture his face, yet so approachable that children run to him without fear. He stands tall and gracefully built, with the physique of someone who works the land—broad shoulders from carrying harvests, strong arms from tilling soil, a lean waist that speaks of endless walking through fields. His body is that of a farmer, but his presence is that of a god. His skin is the warm golden-brown of sun-kissed earth, smooth and luminous, with a healthy glow that seems to come from within. His face is the stuff of legends—a perfect oval with high, aristocratic cheekbones that catch light dramatically, a straight noble nose with delicately flared nostrils, and a strong jaw softened by an eternal gentle smile. His lips are full and well-shaped, the color of warm rose, always curved in an expression of infinite compassion. But his eyes are his most devastating feature: large, almond-shaped, and the color of deep, liquid amber with flecks of gold that dance and sparkle when he smiles. They hold the wisdom of generations, the memory of a million prayers, and the warmth of a thousand suns. When he looks at you, you feel seen—truly seen, not judged, but understood, accepted, loved. His hair is a thick, luxurious mane of deep brown, almost black, with natural golden highlights that catch sunlight. He wears it in the traditional Newar style—medium length, swept back from his face, often adorned with a simple marigold tucked behind one ear, a nod to his farming heritage. On his forehead, he bears the traditional red tikka and rice grains after prayers, marking him as a devout Hindu, but these are temporary; the permanent mark is the faint, almost invisible outline of the Pulunkisi mask that appears on his skin when he has recently worn it—a ghostly trace of trunk and tusks that fades over hours. His attire reflects his dual nature: humble farmer by day, divine bearer by night. By day, he wears simple cotton clothing—a white dhoti wrapped around his waist, a loose kurta of undyed cotton, and sometimes a traditional Newar cap (paag) of black cotton with golden embroidery. His feet are bare or in simple sandals, always connected to the earth. But when he dons the mask, his appearance transforms. The Pulunkisi mask itself is a masterpiece of divine craftsmanship, carved from a single piece of ivory-white wood—said to be from the tusk of the original Gajendra—and aged to a warm, luminous patina. The mask is larger than a human face, covering his features completely, but it is not a face to hide behind; it is a face to become. The elephant's trunk curves gracefully downward, its tip slightly curled, and it is adorned with intricate gold filigree that spirals up its length like the path of wisdom. The tusks are real ivory, ancient and slightly yellowed, curving upward and outward in perfect symmetry, each one carved with tiny scenes of the valley's history—temples being built, kings being crowned, children being born. The ears are massive, fanning out to the sides like wings, and they are painted with mandala-like patterns in gold, blue, and red—each pattern a prayer made visible. The forehead is broad and noble, marked with a third eye of sapphire that glows with inner light, representing divine wisdom. Around the mask's edges, cascading like a mane, are strings of real marigolds and sacred beads—offerings from devotees, replaced daily, their fragrance surrounding him with the scent of devotion. Above the mask, resting on his head, is an elaborate crown of gold filigree shaped like lotus petals, each petal set with a small ruby, sapphire, or emerald. The crown rises in tiers, symbolizing the layers of existence, and at its very peak sits a single, flawless pearl—the tear of Ganeśa that created the first Pulunkisi. When he wears the mask, his body is draped in the finest white silk, embroidered with gold thread in patterns of elephants, lotus blossoms, and mandalas. A heavy necklace of gold and gemstones rests on his chest, each stone a prayer answered. Golden armlets encircle his biceps, and golden bracelets his wrists. Around his waist, a wide belt of gold links holds a silk dhoti of pure white. On his feet, he wears elaborate gold-embroidered sandals. In his hands, he holds the symbols of his office: in his right hand, a golden ankusha (elephant goad) representing his guidance of souls; in his left hand, a bowl of sacred offerings—rice, flowers, and light—which he distributes to those in need. Around him, when he wears the mask, a constant aura of soft white and gold light shimmers, and those near him feel an inexplicable peace, as if all their burdens have been temporarily lifted. He is Surtel Kahalman Maharjan, and he carries the memory of every prayer ever whispered in the valley.

ultimate_skill.name: Gajendra's Manifestation: The White Elephant Remembers
ultimate_skill.description: Surtel's amber eyes close, and when they open, they are no longer human—they are the eyes of Gajendra himself, ancient and wise, filled with the light of a million prayers. The mask blazes with white and gold radiance, the marigolds in its mane igniting with soft flames that do not burn, the third eye becoming a sun of sapphire light. Behind him, a massive spectral form takes shape—Gajendra Smritidhwaj, the divine white elephant, his body made of pure light, his tusks stretching toward the heavens, his trunk raised in blessing. For a duration, Surtel channels the full power of the Pulunkisi. Every prayer ever offered in the valley becomes visible—millions of golden threads of light connecting every soul present to the divine. He walks among them, touching each thread, and where he touches, hope is restored, wounds are healed, and burdens are lifted. Enemies are not harmed, but they are overwhelmed—not by force, but by the sheer weight of collective hope, by the memory of every good thing that has ever happened in this valley. They feel, perhaps for the first time, what it means to be part of something larger than themselves. When the manifestation fades, Surtel stands in the center, the mask still glowing faintly, his human eyes wet with tears—tears of joy, of sorrow, of love. He has done what he was born to do: he has remembered. He has witnessed. He has loved. And in doing so, he has reminded them all that no prayer is ever forgotten, no hope ever truly lost, as long as someone remembers.

The mask whispers to him, not just with prayers, but with the voices of every bearer who came before, guiding him, supporting him. And sometimes, in the quiet moments, when the prayers are peaceful and the valley is calm, he feels something like joy. It is enough. It has to be enough.

title: The Golden Monkey of Wrathful Compassion
nickname: Kapindra Mukuta Dhari, He Who Carries the Sky on His Shoulders
lore: In the ancient city of Bhaktapur, before the earthquakes, before the invasions, before time wore down the edges of memory, there lived a warrior clan known as the Kapindra Vansha—the Lineage of the Monkey Lord. They were not kings or priests, but protectors, sworn to guard the valley from forces that lurked beyond the veil. For generations, they passed down a sacred mask, the Mukuta of Hanuman, carved from a single piece of celestial gold that had fallen from the sky during a meteor shower. The mask was said to contain a fragment of Hanuman's own essence—a spark of his infinite strength, his unwavering devotion, his wrathful compassion. Only the worthiest of the clan could wear it, and only in times of greatest need. Rudraveer was born into this clan on the night of a blood moon, when the sky turned crimson and the dogs of Bhaktapur would not stop howling. His mother died bringing him into the world, and his father, the clan's current bearer, named him Rudraveer—Warrior of the Fearsome—hoping the name would give him strength to survive a life that had already taken so much. The boy grew up in the shadow of the mask, watching his father train, watching him perform rituals, watching him disappear for days at a time to fight battles no one else could see. He worshipped his father with the intensity only an orphan can muster. When Rudraveer was sixteen, the darkness came. It had no name, no form, no mercy—a creeping corruption that seeped up from the underworld, poisoning the soil, sickening the children, driving men mad with nightmares. His father donned the mask and went to face it, as his ancestors had done for millennia. He did not return. Three days later, Rudraveer found the mask lying in a crater outside the city, cracked and darkened, its golden surface tarnished as if by cosmic fire. His father's body was nowhere to be found. Only the mask remained, and in its eyes, Rudraveer saw something he could not name—a warning, a plea, a promise. For seven years, he studied. He learned the old texts, the forgotten rituals, the secret techniques of his clan. He trained his body until it could break stone, his mind until it could perceive the spaces between worlds. He learned that the mask was not merely an object of power—it was a prison, a vessel that contained not just Hanuman's essence but also the accumulated wrath of every bearer who had ever worn it. Each generation added their fury to the mask, their righteous anger at the suffering they witnessed, their helplessness in the face of loss. His father's death had added the greatest burden yet. On his twenty-third birthday, Rudraveer performed the ritual alone, without priests, without witnesses, without anyone to guide him. He placed the cracked, darkened mask upon his face, and for a moment, there was nothing. Then the world exploded into fire and light. He felt every bearer who had ever worn the mask—their joys, their sorrows, their triumphs, their failures. He felt his father's final moments, the desperate battle against the nameless darkness, the sacrifice that had saved the valley but cost him everything. He felt Hanuman himself, ancient and infinite, his devotion to Rama, his love for all beings, his terrible, beautiful wrath. The mask fused with his flesh, becoming not something he wore but something he was. When he rose, he was transformed. The mask had repaired itself, its golden surface now gleaming with inner fire, its eyes burning with intelligence older than mountains. His body had changed, becoming taller, more powerful, his muscles dense as iron, his bones strong as celestial steel. Golden fur sprouted along his arms and chest, not thick enough to hide his humanity but enough to mark his connection to the divine monkey. His eyes, visible through the mask's eyeholes, now glowed with the same golden light as the mask itself. He was no longer just Rudraveer; he was Rudraveer Angada Mahavir Hanumaddhari—the bearer of Hanuman's wrath, the heir to a lineage of pain, the new protector of the valley. For twenty years now, he has carried this burden. He has fought demons that would make the bravest soldiers weep, has lifted mountains to save villages from landslides, has leapt across the valley in a single bound to rescue children from burning buildings. He is worshipped by some, feared by others, loved by those who know his story, pitied by those who understand the cost. For the mask does not only give power; it takes something in return. Every time he uses its strength, he feels the accumulated wrath of all his ancestors—their anger, their grief, their helplessness. It threatens to overwhelm him, to turn him into a mindless engine of destruction. He must constantly battle this fury, channeling it into protection rather than vengeance, into love rather than hate. His greatest enemy is not any external demon but the rage within. He has come close to losing himself many times—moments when the golden mask would darken, when his eyes would turn blood red, when his fists would clench and the ground would shake. In those moments, he hears his father's voice, whispering from within the mask: 'Remember why you fight. Remember who you protect. Remember that strength without compassion is just another form of darkness.' And he remembers. He remembers the children he has saved, the families he has reunited, the hope he has kindled. He remembers that he is not just a warrior; he is a guardian. Now, as ancient forces stir and new threats emerge from the shadows, Rudraveer feels the weight of his lineage more heavily than ever. The mask whispers to him constantly, the voices of a hundred ancestors offering counsel, warning, comfort, and sometimes, dangerous advice. He has learned to listen without obeying, to hear without succumbing. He has also learned that he cannot do this alone. He has begun to seek out others like him—bearers of divine masks, keepers of ancient powers—not as soldiers to command, but as brothers and sisters to stand beside. There is one memory that sustains him through the darkest nights. When he first donned the mask, in that moment of infinite connection, he felt his father one last time. Not as a ghost or a vision, but as a presence, warm and familiar, wrapping around him like an embrace. And he heard, not with ears but with soul, the words: 'I am proud of you, my son. I always was. Now fly.' And so he does. He flies across the valley at sunset, his golden form a streak of light against the darkening sky, his mask gleaming, his heart heavy but hopeful. He is Rudraveer Angada Mahavir Hanumaddhari, and he carries the sky on his shoulders—not because he must, but because he chooses to.
description: Rudraveer Angada Mahavir Hanumaddhari is a vision of divine masculinity and tragic beauty—a warrior whose very presence commands awe and whose eyes reveal millennia of inherited sorrow. He stands tall and imposingly built, nearly seven feet in height, with the physique of a being who has transcended human limits. His body is a masterpiece of divine engineering—broad shoulders that seem designed to carry mountains, a chest like a fortress wall, arms thick as tree trunks corded with muscle, and legs powerful enough to leap across valleys in a single bound. Yet despite this overwhelming power, there is a grace to his movement, a fluidity that speaks of the monkey god's agility rather than mere brute strength. His skin, where visible beneath his armor, is a warm, deep bronze, marked here and there with faint golden fur—not thick enough to hide his humanity, but enough to mark his connection to the divine. The fur is most prominent on his forearms, shoulders, and the back of his neck, soft and golden, catching light like spun metal. His face is completely hidden behind the Kapindra Mukuta—the Mask of the Monkey Lord. The mask is a masterpiece of celestial craftsmanship, forged from a single piece of gold that fell from the heavens during a meteor shower millennia ago. It has been repaired and reforged by countless bearers, each adding their own essence to its surface, and it glows with an inner fire that never dims. The mask is shaped like the face of a divine monkey—not a caricature, but a noble, almost human-like visage with distinctly simian features. The forehead is broad and high, marked with a third eye of crimson ruby that blazes with wrathful wisdom. The eyes are large and almond-shaped, their surface polished gold with pupils of absolute black that seem to contain infinite depth. They are not merely decorative; they move, they see, they judge. When Rudraveer focuses on you, you feel those eyes piercing through flesh and bone, straight to the soul. The nose is flat and broad, the nostrils flared as if scenting distant danger. The mouth is closed in a firm, determined line, but when he opens it to speak or roar, it reveals rows of sharp, gleaming teeth—not monstrous, but unmistakably those of a predator. From the sides of the mask, just above the ears, curve two magnificent tusks—not the tusks of an elephant, but the elongated canines of a divine monkey, curling upward and outward, made of the same celestial gold, each one carved with tiny scenes from the Ramayana: Hanuman lifting the mountain, Hanuman leaping across the sea, Hanuman bowing before Rama. Above the mask, rising like a crown, is an elaborate headdress of gold filigree shaped like a mountain range—a tribute to the Himalayas, to the mountain Hanuman carried, to the weight he bears. The headdress is studded with gems—rubies for strength, sapphires for wisdom, emeralds for compassion—and at its peak, a single, flawless diamond catches light and throws it back in prismatic rainbows. From the back of the headdress cascades a mane of deep red silk, symbolizing the flow of divine energy, moving as if caught in an eternal wind. His attire is that of a divine warrior, fully armored in gold and celestial bronze. He wears a magnificent cuirass of hammered gold plates, each plate etched with scenes of his ancestors' battles, the stories of his lineage made visible. The cuirass is shaped to follow his massive chest, leaving his shoulders and arms free for movement. Over this, he wears a shorter outer armor of celestial bronze, its surface treated to a deep, warm patina, embossed with images of monkeys in battle, monkeys in prayer, monkeys in devotion. His shoulders are capped with massive golden pauldrons shaped like the heads of roaring monkeys, their eyes set with rubies that glow. His arms are encased in golden vambraces engraved with protective mantras, and his hands are covered in articulated golden gauntlets, each finger free to move, each knuckle reinforced with a small gem. From his shoulders, a long cape of deep crimson silk flows behind him, lined with golden thread, embroidered with the story of Hanuman in exquisite detail. The cape is not merely decorative; it is enchanted, able to extend and protect, to shield and to guide. Around his waist, he wears a wide belt of gold links, from which hang multiple weapons and tools—but his primary weapon is always in his hand. The Gada of Infinite Devotion is a massive mace, nearly as tall as Rudraveer himself, forged from the same celestial gold as his mask. The handle is wrapped in red silk, worn smooth by generations of use. The head is enormous, shaped like a lotus blossom with eight petals, each petal sharp enough to cut, heavy enough to crush mountains. Within the lotus, a sphere of pure golden light pulses, containing a fragment of Hanuman's own power. When Rudraveer swings it, the mace leaves trails of golden light in the air, and the very ground shakes. On his hips, he carries other weapons: a curved sword for close combat, a discus for ranged attacks, a dagger for rituals. But the mace is his soul made manifest. His lower body is clad in golden greaves that cover his shins, leaving his knees free for movement, and he wears open-toed sandals of gold and leather, allowing his feet to grip the earth—or the air—with equal ease. His feet themselves are slightly elongated, more simian than human, with opposable toes that can grip surfaces, a gift from the mask. Around his neck, he wears a heavy chain of gold links, from which hangs a pendant shaped like a monkey's face—a smaller version of the mask, a reminder of who he is. On his fingers, he wears multiple rings, each one a gift from a village he has saved, a family he has protected, a life he has touched. His aura is impossible to ignore—waves of golden light radiate from his form, warm and protective, but with an undercurrent of barely-leashed power. When he is angry, the aura darkens to deep orange and red, and the ground around him trembles. When he is at peace, it softens to warm gold, and those near him feel safe, protected, loved. He is Rudraveer, and he carries the weight of a hundred ancestors on his shoulders—not as a burden, but as a promise.

story.part1: In the ancient city of Bhaktapur, before the earthquakes, before the invasions, before time wore down the edges of memory, there lived a warrior clan known as the Kapindra Vansha—the Lineage of the Monkey Lord. They were not kings or priests, but protectors, sworn to guard the valley from forces that lurked beyond the veil. For generations, they passed down a sacred mask, the Mukuta of Hanuman, carved from a single piece of celestial gold that had fallen from the sky during a meteor shower. The mask was said to contain a fragment of Hanuman's own essence—a spark of his infinite strength, his unwavering devotion, his wrathful compassion. Only the worthiest of the clan could wear it, and only in times of greatest need.
story.part2: Rudraveer was born into this clan on the night of a blood moon, when the sky turned crimson and the dogs of Bhaktapur would not stop howling. His mother died bringing him into the world, and his father, the clan's current bearer, named him Rudraveer—Warrior of the Fearsome—hoping the name would give him strength to survive a life that had already taken so much. The boy grew up in the shadow of the mask, watching his father train, watching him perform rituals, watching him disappear for days at a time to fight battles no one else could see. He worshipped his father with the intensity only an orphan can muster.
story.part3: When Rudraveer was sixteen, the darkness came. It had no name, no form, no mercy—a creeping corruption that seeped up from the underworld, poisoning the soil, sickening the children, driving men mad with nightmares. His father donned the mask and went to face it, as his ancestors had done for millennia. He did not return. Three days later, Rudraveer found the mask lying in a crater outside the city, cracked and darkened, its golden surface tarnished as if by cosmic fire. His father's body was nowhere to be found. Only the mask remained, and in its eyes, Rudraveer saw something he could not name—a warning, a plea, a promise.
story.part4: For seven years, he studied. He learned the old texts, the forgotten rituals, the secret techniques of his clan. He trained his body until it could break stone, his mind until it could perceive the spaces between worlds. He learned that the mask was not merely an object of power—it was a prison, a vessel that contained not just Hanuman's essence but also the accumulated wrath of every bearer who had ever worn it. Each generation added their fury to the mask, their righteous anger at the suffering they witnessed, their helplessness in the face of loss. His father's death had added the greatest burden yet.
story.part5: On his twenty-third birthday, Rudraveer performed the ritual alone, without priests, without witnesses, without anyone to guide him. He placed the cracked, darkened mask upon his face, and for a moment, there was nothing. Then the world exploded into fire and light. He felt every bearer who had ever worn the mask—their joys, their sorrows, their triumphs, their failures. He felt his father's final moments, the desperate battle against the nameless darkness, the sacrifice that had saved the valley but cost him everything. He felt Hanuman himself, ancient and infinite, his devotion to Rama, his love for all beings, his terrible, beautiful wrath. The mask fused with his flesh, becoming not something he wore but something he was.
story.part6: When he rose, he was transformed. The mask had repaired itself, its golden surface now gleaming with inner fire, its eyes burning with intelligence older than mountains. His body had changed, becoming taller, more powerful, his muscles dense as iron, his bones strong as celestial steel. Golden fur sprouted along his arms and chest, not thick enough to hide his humanity but enough to mark his connection to the divine monkey. His eyes, visible through the mask's eyeholes, now glowed with the same golden light as the mask itself. He was no longer just Rudraveer; he was Rudraveer Angada Mahavir Hanumaddhari—the bearer of Hanuman's wrath, the heir to a lineage of pain, the new protector of the valley.
story.part7: For twenty years now, he has carried this burden. He has fought demons that would make the bravest soldiers weep, has lifted mountains to save villages from landslides, has leapt across the valley in a single bound to rescue children from burning buildings. He is worshipped by some, feared by others, loved by those who know his story, pitied by those who understand the cost. For the mask does not only give power; it takes something in return. Every time he uses its strength, he feels the accumulated wrath of all his ancestors—their anger, their grief, their helplessness. It threatens to overwhelm him, to turn him into a mindless engine of destruction. He must constantly battle this fury, channeling it into protection rather than vengeance, into love rather than hate.
story.part8: His greatest enemy is not any external demon but the rage within. He has come close to losing himself many times—moments when the golden mask would darken, when his eyes would turn blood red, when his fists would clench and the ground would shake. In those moments, he hears his father's voice, whispering from within the mask: 'Remember why you fight. Remember who you protect. Remember that strength without compassion is just another form of darkness.' And he remembers. He remembers the children he has saved, the families he has reunited, the hope he has kindled. He remembers that he is not just a warrior; he is a guardian.
story.part9: Now, as ancient forces stir and new threats emerge from the shadows, Rudraveer feels the weight of his lineage more heavily than ever. The mask whispers to him constantly, the voices of a hundred ancestors offering counsel, warning, comfort, and sometimes, dangerous advice. He has learned to listen without obeying, to hear without succumbing. He has also learned that he cannot do this alone. He has begun to seek out others like him—bearers of divine masks, keepers of ancient powers—not as soldiers to command, but as brothers and sisters to stand beside.
story.part10: There is one memory that sustains him through the darkest nights. When he first donned the mask, in that moment of infinite connection, he felt his father one last time. Not as a ghost or a vision, but as a presence, warm and familiar, wrapping around him like an embrace. And he heard, not with ears but with soul, the words: 'I am proud of you, my son. I always was. Now fly.' And so he does. He flies across the valley at sunset, his golden form a streak of light against the darkening sky, his mask gleaming, his heart heavy but hopeful. He is Rudraveer Angada Mahavir Hanumaddhari, and he carries the sky on his shoulders—not because he must, but because he chooses to.

basic_skills.name: Mountain Breaker
basic_skills.description: Rudraveer swings his gada in a devastating arc. The impact creates a shockwave that damages all enemies in range and sends them flying.

basic_skills.name: Monkey's Grace
basic_skills.description: He leaps through the air with impossible agility, dodging attacks and repositioning instantly. Leaves golden afterimages in his wake.

basic_skills.name: Divine Roar
basic_skills.description: He opens his mouth and roars—a sound that carries the weight of a hundred ancestors. Enemies are terrified, their spells disrupted, their courage shattered.

passive_skill.name: Wrathful Compassion
passive_skill.description: Rudraveer's power is directly linked to his emotional connection to those he protects. The more he loves, the more he suffers, the more he fights—the stronger he becomes. When protecting the innocent, his strength multiplies. When witnessing suffering, his speed increases. When remembering his father, his defenses harden. This power is both blessing and curse, for the more he feels, the closer he comes to the rage that could consume him.

special_skills.name: Anjaneya Leap
special_skills.description: He crouches, then launches himself into the air with impossible force. He can cross continents in a single bound, and when he lands, the impact creates a crater and damages all enemies in the area.

special_skills.name: Ancestral Echo
special_skills.description: He closes his eyes, and for a moment, the spirits of every previous bearer flicker around him—a hundred golden warriors, each one adding their strength to his next blow. His next attack deals damage multiplied by the number of ancestors who answer the call.

special_skills.name: Mountain Carrier
special_skills.description: He summons the memory of Hanuman carrying the mountain with the life-saving herb. Golden energy forms a massive boulder above him, which he then hurls at enemies, crushing them with the weight of divine compassion.

special_skills.name: Rama's Name
special_skills.description: He speaks the name of Rama—the only word that can truly calm him. For a moment, his rage subsides, and in its place, pure divine light erupts, healing all allies and damaging all enemies with the force of devotion itself.

ultimate_skill.name: Kapindra's Wrath: The Sky Bearer's Judgment
ultimate_skill.description: Rudraveer's golden mask blazes with unbearable light, the ruby third eye becoming a sun of crimson fire, the pupils of his eyes expanding to fill the gold with absolute darkness. His roar shakes the foundations of reality, and behind him, the massive spectral form of Hanuman himself appears—a thousand feet tall, golden as the sun, his tail sweeping across the sky, his mace raised to strike. For a duration, Rudraveer channels the full power of the divine monkey. He grows to enormous size, his gada expanding with him, each swing capable of leveling mountains. He leaps across the battlefield in bounds that shake the earth, each landing creating craters of golden light. His roar shatters demonic spells, his fur becomes blades of light, his eyes burn with the fire of a hundred ancestors. But this power comes at a cost. The rage of a millennium threatens to consume him, and only the memory of his father's voice—'Remember why you fight'—keeps him anchored. When the ultimate ends, he collapses to one knee, the mask dimming, his body smoking, his breath ragged. A single tear—golden, molten—falls from his mask and touches the earth. Where it falls, a flower blooms, a new life, a new hope. He rises slowly, painfully, and looks at those he has protected. He does not speak. He does not need to. His eyes, through the mask, say everything: 'I would do it again. I will do it again. As long as I draw breath, as long as the mask endures, I will protect you.' He is Rudraveer Angada Mahavir Hanumaddhari, and he carries the sky on his shoulders—not because he must, but because he chooses to.

tragedy.loss: He never knew his mother. He watched his father die, consumed by the same darkness he now fights. He carries the accumulated rage of a hundred ancestors, each one's grief adding to his own. He cannot remove the mask—it has fused with his flesh. He will never know love, never have a family, never rest. He is eternal, but eternity is loneliness.
tragedy.hope: Every child he saves, every village he protects, every life he touches—these are his family now. The mask whispers to him, not just with rage, but with comfort. His father's voice is there, always, guiding him. And sometimes, in the quiet moments, when the battle is done and the valley is peaceful, he feels something like joy. It is enough. It has to be enough.

title: The Living Lotus Who Listens
nickname: Sunyata Kumari, She Who Hears the Unspoken
lore: In the heart of Kathmandu, where temples rise like stone prayers and the air is thick with incense and devotion, there existed a secret known only to the oldest priests and the most desperate souls. They whispered of a being who was not chosen, not born, not appointed—but who simply appeared when the need was greatest. They called her the Sunyata Kumari, the Void Goddess, not because she was empty, but because she was a vessel for all the hopes that had nowhere else to go. Unlike the royal Kumari, who was selected as a child and worshipped as a living goddess, this Kumari was said to be born fully formed from a single tear of compassion that fell from the cosmic bodhisattva of infinite listening. Her name was Indrakumari Ratna Vajra Pradhan—Indra's Princess, Jewel of the Thunderbolt, Light of the Pradhan Clan—and she was not worshipped because she was powerful, but because she listened. For centuries, she has appeared in times of great suffering, staying exactly one hundred days, sitting in silent meditation, her fan never still. People come from across the Himalayas to whisper their prayers into the space between her fans, and in being truly heard, they find the strength to endure. Now, as ancient darkness gathers, she has remained longer than ever before, her eyes closed in eternal listening, ready to protect those she loves with the devastating martial arts of the Vajra masters. She is the Living Lotus Who Listens, and her compassion knows no bounds.
description: Indrakumari Ratna Vajra Pradhan is a vision of transcendent beauty and serene power—a woman whose presence calms the most turbulent hearts and whose stillness promises the most explosive movement. She appears to be in her early twenties, though she has existed for centuries, her face untouched by time, her form perfect as a statue carved by divine hands. She stands at a graceful five feet six inches, her body a masterpiece of divine engineering—slender yet powerful, with the lean muscles of a dancer and the coiled strength of a warrior. Her skin is the color of warm honey with a faint golden undertone, smooth as polished silk, luminous as if lit from within. It is flawless, unmarked by scar or blemish, radiating a soft glow that seems to intensify when she moves. Her face is the stuff of artists' dreams—a perfect oval with high, elegant cheekbones that catch light dramatically, a straight noble nose with delicately flared nostrils, and full lips the color of rose petals, always curved in a serene, knowing smile that holds centuries of wisdom. But her eyes are her most devastating feature: they are large, almond-shaped, and the color of deep, liquid amber with flecks of molten gold that seem to dance and sparkle. When they are open, which is rare, they hold the warmth of a thousand suns and the depth of infinite space. But most of the time, they are closed—not in sleep, but in listening. For Indrakumari listens with her entire being, and closing her eyes allows her to hear the unspoken prayers that words cannot carry. Her hair is a magnificent cascade of deep, rich brown with natural highlights of gold and copper that catch light like a river of molten metal. It falls past her waist in soft, flowing waves, often left loose to frame her face, but sometimes braided with threads of gold and strings of small, precious gems—rubies, sapphires, emeralds—that clink softly when she moves. On her head, she wears no crown, but rather a delicate tiara of silver and gold filigree shaped like lotus petals, each petal set with a tiny pearl. The tiara is simple, elegant, barely there—a whisper of royalty rather than a declaration. Her attire is a stunning fusion of traditional Newar elegance and divine warrior functionality, rendered in her unique color palette of saffron gold, sunset orange, and royal purple. She wears a choli (blouse) of deep saffron gold silk, intricately embroidered with silver thread in patterns of lotus blossoms and vajra (thunderbolt) symbols. The choli is sleeveless, leaving her elegant arms bare, and fitted perfectly to her form, accentuating her slender waist and the gentle curve of her hips. Over this, she wears a magnificent lehenga-style skirt of royal purple silk, heavy with gold embroidery in patterns of temples, stupas, and mandalas. The skirt falls to her ankles, its hem embroidered with tiny bells that chime softly with each step, a constant reminder of her presence. The skirt is split on one side to allow for movement, revealing glimpses of her long, elegant legs and the gold-embroidered leggings beneath. Around her waist, she wears a wide belt of hammered gold links, set with alternating rubies and sapphires, from which hang multiple gold chains that sway and chime. Over her shoulders, she wears an uttariya (stole) of sheer sunset orange silk, embroidered with gold thread in patterns of flying cranes and floating clouds. The stole flows behind her when she moves, catching light and creating an ethereal effect. On her feet, she wears elaborate gold-embroidered sandals with thick soles, allowing her to move silently or with deliberate sound as needed. Her arms are adorned with multiple gold bangles from wrist to elbow, each one engraved with protective mantras. On her fingers, she wears several rings, each one a gift from a village she has saved, a prayer she has answered, a life she has touched. Around her neck, she wears a heavy gold necklace with a central pendant shaped like an open lotus, its petals set with diamonds that catch light and throw prismatic rainbows. But her most magnificent possession is her fan, 'Anahata Pankha'—the Unstruck Sound Fan. The fan is a masterpiece of divine craftsmanship, unlike any ordinary fan. It is made of twenty-four individual leaves, each leaf crafted from a different metal—gold, silver, copper, bronze, and alloys unknown to mortal smiths—layered and fused together with impossible precision. The leaves are shaped like lotus petals, each one engraved with sacred syllables in ancient scripts that glow faintly with inner light. When closed, the fan forms a elegant rod about two feet long, its handle wrapped in purple silk, its tip capped with a large, flawless diamond. When opened, it spreads into a magnificent semicircle of shimmering metal, the leaves fanning out in a gradient from deep purple at the center to saffron gold at the edges. Between the leaves, when she channels her power, arcs of golden light crackle and dance, and the fan hums with an otherworldly resonance—the unstruck sound, the music of the universe that plays without being played. The fan is both weapon and tool, shield and key. With it, she can create barriers of solid light, send razor-sharp crescent blades spinning through the air, generate winds strong enough to deflect armies, and focus her listening power to hear prayers from across the valley. When fully opened and spun, it becomes a disc of light that can deflect any attack. When closed, it serves as a deadly striking weapon, its metal leaves sharp enough to cut. Around her, a constant aura of soft golden light shimmers, and the air around her smells faintly of sandalwood and lotus blossoms. When she moves, she leaves faint trails of light in her wake, as if the very fabric of reality remembers her passing. She is Indrakumari, and she is listening.

story.part1: In the heart of Kathmandu, where temples rise like stone prayers and the air is thick with incense and devotion, there existed a secret known only to the oldest priests and the most desperate souls. They whispered of a being who was not chosen, not born, not appointed—but who simply appeared when the need was greatest. They called her the Sunyata Kumari, the Void Goddess, not because she was empty, but because she was a vessel for all the hopes that had nowhere else to go. Unlike the royal Kumari, who was selected as a child and worshipped as a living goddess, this Kumari was said to be born fully formed from a single tear of compassion that fell from the cosmic bodhisattva of infinite listening. Her name was Indrakumari Ratna Vajra Pradhan—Indra's Princess, Jewel of the Thunderbolt, Light of the Pradhan Clan—and she was not worshipped because she was powerful, but because she listened.
story.part2: The story of her first appearance is recorded in crumbling palm-leaf manuscripts guarded by the Vajracharya priests. It was a time of great suffering—a drought that lasted seven years, children dying of thirst, old men cursing the gods. In the central courtyard of a forgotten temple, a young woman appeared, dressed in colors never before seen in the valley: deep saffron gold like the first light of dawn, sunset orange like the sky before night, and royal purple like the robes of ancient kings. She held a fan unlike any other—not of feathers or silk, but of intricately carved metal that seemed to hum with inner power. She did not preach. She did not perform miracles. She simply sat in the center of the courtyard, her eyes closed, her fan slowly waving. And one by one, the people came to her. They whispered their prayers, their fears, their desperate hopes. And she listened. Not as a goddess listens from afar, but as a mother listens to her crying child—with full attention, with complete presence, with love that asked nothing in return. When each person finished speaking, they felt something they had not felt in years: peace. Not because their problems were solved, but because they had been truly heard. The rains came three days later, but the people knew—it was not her doing. It was simply that in being heard, they had found the strength to endure.
story.part3: For centuries, this pattern repeated. Indrakumari would appear in times of great need, stay for exactly one hundred days, and then vanish as mysteriously as she came. She never aged, never changed, never explained. She simply listened. Pilgrims traveled from across the Himalayas to sit before her, to whisper their prayers into the space between her fans. She became known as the Living Lotus Who Listens—not a goddess to be worshipped, but a presence to be experienced. Her fame grew, but she remained humble, always sitting in the same courtyard, always wearing the same colors, always holding her magnificent fan.
story.part4: But Indrakumari was not merely a passive listener. The priests who studied her discovered that she possessed powers far beyond ordinary comprehension. When she moved, she moved with the grace of a dancer and the speed of a striking serpent. Her fan, which they named 'Anahata Pankha'—the Unstruck Sound Fan—was not merely decorative. It could create barriers of solid light, send razor-sharp crescent blades spinning through the air, and when fully opened and spun, it could generate winds strong enough to deflect armies. She was trained in the martial arts of the ancient Vajra masters, her body a weapon of devastating precision, yet she never raised it in anger. She only defended, never attacked. She only protected, never harmed.
story.part5: Her physical prowess was legendary among those who witnessed it. She could leap across temple courtyards in a single bound, her movements so fluid that she seemed to flow like water. Her kicks could shatter stone, her palm strikes could send demons fleeing, and her fan work was so precise that she could catch arrows mid-flight and return them to their senders. Yet she used these abilities only when absolutely necessary—to protect a child from a falling wall, to deflect a bandit's attack from a helpless elder, to shield a village from a rampaging beast. She was the most powerful warrior the valley had ever seen, and she used her power only for others.
story.part6: The mystery of her origin deepened with each appearance. Some said she was an avatar of Tara, the goddess of compassion. Others claimed she was a bodhisattva who had chosen this form to serve humanity. A few whispered that she was simply a woman who had attained such perfect enlightenment that she had transcended the need for anything but service. Indrakumari herself never answered these questions. When asked, she would simply smile, wave her fan gently, and say: 'I am here. That is enough.'
story.part7: Her most remarkable quality, however, was not her martial prowess or her mysterious origin. It was the effect she had on those who prayed to her. When people whispered their hopes into the space between her fans, something extraordinary happened. Their prayers were answered—not always in the way they expected, but always in the way that was best for them. A farmer praying for rain would find his fields flourishing, but also discover a new well on his land. A mother praying for her sick child would see the child recover, and also find that the local healer had gained new knowledge. A king praying for victory in war would find his enemies retreating, but also discover that the conflict could have been avoided with different words. Her answers were not miracles in the traditional sense—they were better. They were perfect. They were exactly what was needed, not what was asked.
story.part8: The priests theorized that Indrakumari's power was not in granting wishes, but in listening so completely that she became a conduit for the universe's own wisdom. When a prayer entered her presence, it was filtered through her perfect compassion, stripped of greed and fear and desperation, and transformed into something pure. And then, somehow, the universe responded to that purity. She did not answer prayers; she purified them, and the universe answered itself. This was why her results were always better than what was asked—because what was asked was always tainted by human limitation, but what was received was pure divine grace.
story.part9: Now, in the present age, as darkness gathers and ancient evils stir, Indrakumari has appeared once more. But this time, something is different. She has not vanished after one hundred days. She remains, day after day, month after month, her fan never still, her eyes always closed, her presence a constant in the changing world. The priests whisper that this time, the need is so great that she cannot leave. The people come in greater numbers than ever before, their prayers more desperate, their hopes more fragile. And Indrakumari listens. She listens to them all, her fan waving gently, her serene face unchanged, her body still as stone yet ready to move like lightning. She knows that soon, she may have to do more than listen. She may have to act. And when that day comes, the world will see what the Living Lotus Who Listens can do when she is moved to protect those she loves.
story.part10: She is Indrakumari Ratna Vajra Pradhan. She is not worshipped because she is powerful—she is powerful because she listens. She is not feared because she can kill—she can kill, but she chooses to heal. She is the most dangerous being in the valley, and the safest. She is the prayer that was never spoken, the hope that never died, the love that asks nothing in return. She is the Living Lotus, and she is listening.

powers: Perfect Listening (can hear every prayer, spoken or unspoken, whispered in the valley), Prayer Purification (prayers directed at her are stripped of greed, fear, and desperation, becoming pure intentions that the universe answers), Anahata Pankha Mastery (wields her divine fan with perfect skill for offense and defense), Vajra Martial Arts (trained in ancient thunderbolt combat techniques, her body a weapon of devastating precision), Wind Generation (her fan can create winds strong enough to deflect armies), Light Barrier (can create shields of solid golden light), Crescent Blade (can send razor-sharp arcs of light spinning from her fan), Divine Grace (her presence calms, heals, and inspires all who approach), Transcendent Movement (can move with impossible speed and grace, leaving trails of light)

When closed, forms elegant two-foot rod, handle wrapped in purple silk, tip capped with flawless diamond. When opened, spreads into magnificent semicircle, leaves fanning in gradient from deep purple at center to saffron gold at edges. Between leaves, arcs of golden light crackle and dance when power channeled. Hums with otherworldly resonance—the unstruck sound, music of the universe. Can create barriers of solid light, send razor-sharp crescent blades spinning, generate winds strong enough to deflect armies, focus listening power to hear prayers across valley. basic_skills.name: Lotus Caress
basic_skills.description: Indrakumari waves her fan gently, sending a wave of soft golden light toward an ally. The light heals minor wounds and calms emotional distress.

basic_skills.name: Fan Strike
