basic_skills.name: Listening Presence
basic_skills.description: She closes her eyes and tilts her head slightly. For a moment, all within range feel as if their deepest thoughts are heard and understood. Allies gain courage; enemies feel exposed and hesitant.

passive_skill.name: Aura of Perfect Listening
passive_skill.description: Indrakumari constantly radiates an aura of profound attention and compassion. Within her vicinity, all beings feel heard, understood, and valued. Fear diminishes, hope strengthens, and even the most hardened hearts soften. Those who speak to her—even silently—find their words received with perfect attention. This aura extends beyond physical presence; prayers directed at her from anywhere in the valley are heard and held in her consciousness.

special_skills.name: Lotus Barrier
special_skills.description: She opens her fan fully and sweeps it in an arc before her. A translucent barrier of golden light shaped like lotus petals expands, protecting herself and allies from all incoming attacks. The barrier absorbs damage and gently repels enemies who touch it.

special_skills.name: Crescent Arc
special_skills.description: She flicks her wrist, and from her fan, a razor-sharp crescent blade of golden light spins through the air. The blade can strike multiple enemies in a line, slicing through armor and magic alike before dissipating.

special_skills.name: Wind of Compassion
special_skills.description: She fans rapidly, generating a gentle but irresistible wind that flows from her. Allies are pushed toward safety; enemies are pushed back, disoriented by the warm, fragrant breeze that carries the scent of lotus and sandalwood.

special_skills.name: Listening Focus
special_skills.description: She closes her eyes and holds her fan before her face. For a moment, she can hear every prayer, every hope, every fear in the valley. She can then choose to amplify one prayer, granting it to the universe with such clarity that it cannot be ignored.

ultimate_skill.name: Sunyata Kumari's Judgment: The Unstruck Sound
ultimate_skill.description: Indrakumari's eyes—usually closed—slowly open, and when they do, they are no longer merely amber. They are pools of infinite golden light, containing the wisdom of ages and the compassion of all bodhisattvas. Her fan unfolds to its full span, the twenty-four leaves separating into a perfect circle around her, each leaf hovering independently, forming a mandala of spinning metal and light. The unstruck sound becomes audible—a deep, resonant hum that vibrates through every cell, every atom, every soul. From her, waves of pure golden light expand in all directions, and in that light, every prayer ever whispered in the valley becomes visible—millions of threads of light, each one a hope, a fear, a desperate wish, a quiet gratitude. She reaches out with her consciousness and touches each thread, not to answer them, but to hold them, to acknowledge them, to let each soul know that they are not forgotten. Enemies caught in this light are not harmed, but they are overwhelmed—not by force, but by the sheer weight of being truly heard, truly seen, truly understood for the first time in their lives. They weep. They kneel. They remember who they were before hatred consumed them. Allies are filled with such profound peace and purpose that they become unstoppable, their hearts aligned with the universe itself. When the light fades, Indrakumari stands at the center, her fan slowly closing, her eyes closing once more, a single tear of golden light tracing down her cheek—not of sorrow, but of joy. She has listened. She has heard. She has loved. And in doing so, she has reminded them all that the greatest power in the universe is not the ability to destroy, but the willingness to hear. She is Indrakumari Ratna Vajra Pradhan, the Living Lotus Who Listens, and she will never stop listening.

tragedy.loss: She hears every prayer, every hope, every fear—but she cannot answer them all. She carries the weight of every unfulfilled wish, every desperate cry that went unanswered, every soul who prayed and was not saved. This weight would crush any ordinary being, but Indrakumari has learned to transform it into fuel for her compassion. Still, there are nights when she sits alone, her fan still, and weeps for those she could not help.
tragedy.hope: Every soul she touches, every prayer she holds, every being she comforts—these are her family. She is not alone, for she carries the hopes of millions within her. And sometimes, in the quiet moments between prayers, she feels something like joy—not for herself, but for the beauty of existence, for the courage of those who hope despite everything. It is enough. It will always be enough.

title: The Gilded Lotus of Bhaktapur
nickname: Nritya Devi, She Who Dances Between Worlds
lore: In the ancient city of Bhaktapur, where every brick is a prayer and every courtyard holds a century of footsteps, there lived a family of the Maharjan clan—farmers by trade, but artists by soul. For generations, they had tended the fields that fed the valley, but their true legacy was hidden in their blood: the gift of Nritya Siddhi, the Power of Divine Dance. It was said that when the gods created the world, they danced it into existence, and fragments of that primordial choreography scattered across the cosmos, finding homes in certain bloodlines. The Maharjan of Bhaktapur were one such bloodline, and every generation produced one dancer who could channel the cosmic rhythm. Rabjinah was that dancer for her generation, but unlike her ancestors, she did not discover her gift through ritual or training. She discovered it through tragedy. When she was twelve years old, a catastrophic earthquake struck the valley, toppling temples, burying homes, and separating her from her family. For three days, she was trapped beneath rubble, alone in the darkness, listening to the screams of the dying and the creaking of broken stone. She should have died—of thirst, of fear, of despair. But in that darkness, she heard something else: a rhythm, deep and primal, pulsing from the earth itself. It was the heartbeat of the valley, the drumbeat of creation that had been playing since the first mountain rose. And without thinking, she began to move. Trapped, crushed, barely able to breathe, she danced—not with her body, which could not move, but with her soul. She danced the dance of the earth, the dance of survival, the dance of hope. And the earth heard her. The rubble shifted, creating a pocket of air. A water pipe burst nearby, providing drink. And on the third day, rescuers found her alive, the only survivor from her entire neighborhood. Her family was gone—father, mother, younger brother—all taken by the quake. But Rabjinah remained, and she knew why. The dance had chosen her. For the next ten years, she trained with the surviving elders of her clan, learning the sacred choreographies that had been passed down for millennia. She learned that her dance was not mere performance—it was magic. Each movement could heal or harm, could build or destroy, could call the gods or banish demons. The Ghatu dance could make crops grow; the Dasha Avatar could summon the power of Vishnu's incarnations; the Lakhey dance could channel the fierce protective energy of the demon-deities. And her body, already blessed with the generous curves of her Newar heritage—the narrow waist, the full hips, the powerful thighs, the ample bosom—became a weapon and a temple, each curve accentuated by the traditional Haku Patasi she wore, the black sari with red border that marked her as a woman of the valley. But Rabjinah was not content to simply preserve the old ways. She had seen too much death, lost too much, to simply repeat what had come before. She began to innovate, to create new dances, new movements, new rhythms. She danced with fire and found she could control it. She danced with water and found she could part it. She danced in the cemeteries at night and found she could speak with the dead—including her own family, who visited her in dreams, their spirits comforted by her movements. Her reputation grew, first in Bhaktapur, then across the valley, then beyond. People came from distant lands to witness the dancer whose movements could heal the sick, whose spins could summon rain, whose stamping feet could make the earth tremble. She became known as Nritya Devi—the Dance Goddess—though she never claimed divinity. She was simply Rabjinah, a woman who had learned to dance with the cosmos. Now, at twenty-six, she stands as one of the most powerful beings in the valley, though she rarely leaves Bhaktapur. Her power is not in weapons or armies, but in rhythm and movement. She can heal with a twirl, protect with a stance, and destroy with a stamp. Her body, sculpted by years of dance, moves with impossible grace—every curve, every muscle, every gesture perfectly controlled. She wears the traditional Haku Patasi, the black sari with red border, but hers is no ordinary garment. It is woven with threads of gold and silver, enchanted by generations of dancers, and it flows around her like living shadow, the red border flashing like fire when she spins. Her blouse is of deep crimson silk, embroidered with tiny bells that chime with every breath. Around her neck, she wears the Tayo—a massive, elaborate gold necklace with multiple layers, each layer representing a generation of Maharjan dancers before her. The Tayo is heavy, both physically and spiritually, carrying the weight of her ancestry. On her forehead, she wears a Sirbandi, a gold headpiece with a large red gem at its center, marking her as a married woman—married not to a man, but to the dance itself. Her ears are adorned with Chandra earrings, moon-shaped gold pieces that brush her shoulders. On her arms, she wears multiple gold bangles, each one engraved with a different rhythm, a different dance. Her wrists are encircled by Mundi Mala, gold bead bracelets that click together when she moves, adding percussion to her performance. Her fingers are covered in rings, each one a gift from a village she has saved, a life she has touched. On her feet, she wears gold-embroidered sandals when walking, but when she dances, she is barefoot, her soles connecting directly to the earth, feeling its every vibration. In her hands, she carries no weapon—for her body is her weapon. But when she needs to focus her power, she uses her Chandrahar, a crescent-moon-shaped ornament that she wears as a belt, which can extend into a whip of pure light. She is Rabjinah Maharjan, the Gilded Lotus of Bhaktapur, and she dances not for applause, but for the dead, for the living, for the valley itself.
description: Rabjinah Maharjan is a vision of Newar beauty and divine grace—a woman whose very presence commands attention and whose movements tell stories older than memory. She stands at five feet five inches, her body a masterpiece of feminine curves and dancer's strength. Her figure is the idealized Newar silhouette: a narrow waist that seems almost impossibly small, accentuated by the tight-fitting cholo (blouse) and the way the Haku Patasi wraps around her hips; hips that flare generously, curved and full, supporting the weight of her elaborate sari; thighs thick and powerful, sculpted by years of dancing on stone temple floors, their strength visible even through the folds of fabric; and a bosom full and magnificent, straining against the crimson silk of her cholo, the upper curves visible above the neckline, a testament to her womanhood and her vitality. Her skin is the color of warm honey with golden undertones, smooth as polished bronze, luminous and flawless, with a healthy glow that seems to radiate from within. Years of dancing in the sun have given it a warm, sun-kissed quality, but it remains unblemished, perfect. Her face is a study in classical Newar beauty—a perfect oval with high, sweeping cheekbones that catch light dramatically, a straight noble nose with delicately flared nostrils, and full lips the color of ripe pomegranates, always curved in a serene, knowing smile that holds the wisdom of generations. But her eyes are her most captivating feature: they are large, almond-shaped, and the color of deep, liquid obsidian—so dark they seem to absorb light—yet flecked with tiny gold specks that catch fire when she dances. They hold the depth of centuries, the memory of earthquakes and festivals, of loss and love, of a valley that has seen everything. When she looks at you, you feel as if you are being seen by all her ancestors at once. Her hair is a magnificent cascade of jet-black silk, so long it falls past her waist, straight and thick, with natural waves that catch light and create movement even when she is still. It is always oiled and gleaming, scented with jasmine and sandalwood, and often adorned with fresh flowers—marigolds, roses, or the white champaca—tucked behind her ear or woven into a single braid that hangs over her shoulder. On special occasions, she wears it loose, and it flows around her like a river of night. On her forehead, she wears the Sirbandi, an elaborate gold headpiece that sits at her hairline, its central feature a large, faceted ruby that glows with inner light. The Sirbandi is made of delicate gold chains that drape across her forehead, each chain ending in tiny pearl drops that sway with her movements. It marks her as a married woman—married to her art, to her ancestors, to the dance itself. Above it, sometimes, she wears fresh flowers tucked into her hair. Her ears are adorned with Chandra earrings—large, crescent-moon-shaped gold pieces that hang from her lobes and brush against her shoulders. Each earring is intricately carved with scenes from the Mahabharata, tiny warriors and gods frozen in gold, and they catch light and swing hypnotically when she moves. Around her neck, she wears the Tayo—the most magnificent piece of Newar jewelry, a necklace of such elaborate craftsmanship that it is said to contain the souls of all the Maharjan dancers who came before her. The Tayo is composed of multiple layers of gold chains, each layer heavier and more ornate than the last. The top layer is delicate, with tiny pearls and rubies; the middle layer features large, faceted emeralds and sapphires; the bottom layer is a solid gold plate, intricately carved with the story of the valley's creation. The Tayo covers much of her upper chest, resting just above the swell of her bosom, its weight a constant reminder of her lineage. On her arms, from wrist to elbow, she wears multiple gold bangles—some plain, some engraved, some set with tiny gems. There are at least twenty on each arm, and they clink and chime with every gesture, creating a constant, gentle percussion that accompanies her movements. Each bangle is engraved with a different rhythm, a different dance, a different prayer. On her wrists, she wears Mundi Mala—strands of gold beads that wrap multiple times around, clicking together when she moves her hands. On her fingers, she wears numerous rings—simple gold bands, rings with small gems, rings engraved with mantras—each one a gift from a village she has saved, a family she has healed, a life she has touched. Around her waist, she wears a Chandrahar—a crescent-moon-shaped belt of hammered gold, set with rubies and diamonds, that cinches her already narrow waist and emphasizes the flare of her hips. The Chandrahar is not merely decorative; when she channels her power, it can extend into a whip of pure golden light, a weapon as beautiful as it is deadly. Her attire is the traditional Haku Patasi of Newar women, but elevated to divine status. The sari itself is of the finest black silk, so deep and rich that it seems to absorb light, creating a void against which her golden jewelry blazes. The border is a band of deep crimson, a handspan wide, embroidered with gold thread in patterns of temples, lotus blossoms, and dancing figures. The sari is wrapped in the traditional Newar style, with the pleats falling in front and the pallu (the loose end) draped over her left shoulder and down her back, the crimson border creating a striking diagonal line across her torso. Beneath the sari, she wears a cholo (blouse) of deep crimson silk, fitted perfectly to her form, its neckline cut low enough to reveal the upper curves of her full bosom, a tasteful display of her womanhood. The cholo is sleeveless, leaving her arms bare to display her bangles, and its back is cut low, revealing the smooth expanse of her upper back. The cholo is embroidered with gold thread in patterns of tiny bells and musical notes, and sewn into the fabric are dozens of tiny, real bells that chime with every breath, every movement, creating a constant, subtle music. On her feet, when she is not dancing, she wears elaborate gold-embroidered sandals with thick soles, the leather straps covered in gold thread, the soles allowing her to walk silently or with deliberate sound as needed. But when she dances, she is barefoot, her soles directly connected to the earth, feeling its every vibration, its every pulse. Her feet themselves are works of art—strong and calloused from years of dancing, yet elegant, with long toes and high arches, adorned with small gold rings on each toe. Around her ankles, she wears payal—silver anklets with dozens of tiny bells that chime with every step, adding to the percussion of her movement. She carries no weapon in her hands, for her body is her weapon. But when she needs to fight at range, she can detach her Chandrahar belt and wield it as a whip of pure golden light, its crescent-moon tip sharp enough to cut through steel. And when she dances in truth, her movements themselves become weapons—a spin that generates winds strong enough to deflect arrows, a stamp that creates shockwaves, a gesture that sends arcs of golden light flying. She is Rabjinah Maharjan, and she is the dance made flesh.

story.part1: Rabjinah was born in Bhaktapur, in a traditional Newar house with a courtyard where her grandmother would dance every morning at sunrise. Her earliest memories are of waking to the sound of anklets, of watching the old woman's feet trace patterns on the stone, of feeling the rhythm in her bones before she could walk. Her grandmother told her that the Maharjan blood carried the dance of the gods, and that one day, she would have to choose—to dance for herself, or to dance for the valley.
story.part2: She chose without knowing she was choosing. When the earthquake came, she was twelve, playing in the courtyard while her mother cooked and her father worked in the fields. The ground lurched, and the world ended. She remembers falling, remembers darkness, remembers the weight of stone on her legs. For three days, she lay trapped, listening to the screams fade, listening to the silence grow. And then she heard the rhythm—the heartbeat of the earth itself, deep and primal and eternal. She began to move, trapped as she was, dancing with her soul. And the earth heard her.
story.part3: When they pulled her from the rubble, she was the only survivor from her neighborhood. Her family was gone—all of them. The elders of the Maharjan clan came to her and told her that the dance had chosen her, that she was now the vessel of their lineage. She did not understand, but she agreed to learn. What else could she do? She had nothing left but the rhythm in her bones.
story.part4: For ten years, she trained. She learned the Ghatu dance that makes crops grow, the Dasha Avatar that channels Vishnu's power, the Lakhey dance that summons demon-protectors. She learned that each movement was a prayer, each gesture a spell, each rhythm a key to unlocking the universe. Her body changed, grew stronger, more curved, more powerful. The elders said she was the most gifted dancer in a millennium, that her hips could sway the gods themselves, that her feet could make the mountains dance.
story.part5: But Rabjinah was not content with the old dances. She had seen too much death, lost too much, to simply repeat. She began to create—new movements, new rhythms, new dances. She danced in the cremation grounds and found she could speak with the dead. She danced in the fields and found she could make barren soil bloom. She danced in the temples and found that the gods themselves would watch, their stone faces softening, their eyes following her movements.
story.part6: Her reputation grew. People came from across the valley to witness the dancer whose movements could heal, whose spins could summon rain. She never charged, never asked for anything. She simply danced, and in dancing, she gave. She became known as Nritya Devi—the Dance Goddess—though she never claimed the title. She was simply Rabjinah, a woman who had learned to dance with the cosmos.
story.part7: But power attracts attention, not all of it welcome. A sorcerer from the western hills, jealous of her fame, sent demons to attack her village. Rabjinah faced them in the courtyard where her grandmother once danced. She wore only her Haku Patasi, her gold jewelry, and her bare feet. She began to dance—the Lakhey dance, the dance of the demon-protectors. But she did not summon Lakhey; she became one. Her movements grew fierce, her eyes blazed, her stamping feet shook the ground. The demons fled, howling, and the sorcerer's power broke. That night, the villagers rebuilt the shrine in her honor, though she begged them not to.
story.part8: Now, at twenty-six, she is the most powerful being in Bhaktapur, though she still lives in the same simple house, still wakes at sunrise to dance in the courtyard. She has been offered marriage many times—by princes, by merchants, by warriors. She has refused them all. She is married to the dance, she says, and the dance is enough. But sometimes, late at night, when the moon is full and the valley is silent, she dances for her family—for her grandmother, her mother, her father, her little brother. She dances their favorite dances, the ones they taught her, and she swears she can feel them watching, their spirits swaying with her, their love surrounding her like the rhythm of the earth.
story.part9: A new threat has emerged from the shadows of the valley—a force of chaos that seeks to unmake the dance itself, to silence the rhythm of creation. Rabjinah feels it in her bones, in the way the earth's heartbeat has grown erratic, in the way her movements no longer flow as freely. She knows that soon, she will have to dance the greatest dance of her life—not for healing, not for rain, not even for protection, but for the survival of the dance itself. She is ready. She has been ready since she was twelve years old, trapped in the darkness, learning to move when she could not move.
story.part10: She is Rabjinah Maharjan, the Gilded Lotus of Bhaktapur, the Nritya Devi. She does not fight with swords or spells. She fights with rhythm, with movement, with the power of dance that has been in her blood since before she was born. She will dance until the earth stops trembling, until the chaos subsides, until the rhythm returns. And if she falls, she will fall dancing, her last movement a prayer, her last breath a note in the eternal symphony. She is the dance, and the dance will never die.

The Chandrahar belt she wears can detach and extend into a whip of pure golden light, its crescent-moon tip sharp enough to cut through steel. When she dances in truth, her spins generate tornadic winds, her stamps create earthquakes, her gestures send arcs of light flying. The dance itself is the weapon—ancient choreographies passed down for millennia, each one a key to unlocking different magical effects.

Within her vicinity, allies find their movements becoming more coordinated, their timing perfect, as if they are dancing to the same rhythm.

special_skills.name: Ghatu Dance: Dance of Growth
special_skills.description: She performs the ancient Ghatu dance, a slow, undulating movement that mimics the growth of crops. Green light radiates from her footsteps, and where it touches, plants bloom, wounds heal, and allies are refreshed. The dance can cover a large area if she continues it long enough.

special_skills.name: Lakhey Dance: Dance of Protection
special_skills.description: Her movements become fierce, aggressive, her eyes blazing, her stamps shaking the ground. She channels the energy of the Lakhey—the demon-protectors of Newar mythology. For a duration, she gains immense strength and resilience, her attacks dealing bonus damage, and her very presence terrifying enemies.

special_skills.name: Chandrahar Whip
special_skills.description: She detaches her belt and flicks it, the Chandrahar extending into a twenty-foot whip of pure golden light. She can strike multiple enemies with precision, the crescent-moon tip sharp enough to cut through armor, and each lash leaves a trail of light that lingers.

special_skills.name: Ancestral Dance
special_skills.description: She closes her eyes and begins to dance, but the movements are not hers—they are the movements of her ancestors, channeled through her. For a moment, the spirits of every Maharjan dancer who came before her flicker around her, each one adding their power to her next move. Her next dance sequence deals massive damage and cannot be interrupted.

ultimate_skill.name: Nritya Devi's Judgment: Dance of Cosmic Rhythm
ultimate_skill.description: Rabjinah's obsidian eyes blaze with golden light, and for a moment, she is perfectly still—a statue of black and gold. Then she begins to move, and the universe moves with her. She dances the dance that was danced at the beginning of creation, the primordial rhythm that set the cosmos in motion. With each step, waves of golden light expand outward. With each spin, tornados of pure energy spiral across the battlefield. With each gesture, arcs of light strike enemies with precision. The very earth beneath her feet reshapes itself, rising and falling with her rhythm. For the duration of the dance, she is untouchable, moving so fast she leaves afterimages, striking so precisely that no enemy can evade. But the dance is not merely destructive—where her feet touch, flowers bloom; where her hands pass, wounds heal. Allies find themselves moving in perfect sync with her, their attacks timed to perfection, their defenses unbreachable. When the final note of the rhythm sounds and she stops, she stands in the center of a transformed battlefield—enemies defeated, allies triumphant, and the very ground reshaped into the pattern of her dance. A single tear of golden light traces down her cheek—not of sorrow, but of the overwhelming beauty of existence. She has danced the dance of creation, and for one eternal moment, the world was perfect. She is Rabjinah Maharjan, the Gilded Lotus of Bhaktapur, and the dance will never end.

tragedy.loss: She lost her entire family in the earthquake that nearly killed her—father, mother, younger brother. She carries their memory in every movement, dances for them every night, but they never dance back. The weight of being the sole survivor, the only one left to carry her family's legacy, is a burden she bears with grace but never forgets.
tragedy.hope: Every person she heals, every village she protects, every life she touches—these are her family now. The ancestors dance through her, guiding her, supporting her. And sometimes, in the deepest part of the night, when she dances the dances they taught her, she feels them with her—not as memories, but as presences, warm and loving, dancing beside her. It is enough. It will always be enough.

title: The Thunder Drum of Bhaktapur
nickname: Dhimay Bhairav, He Who Beats the Heart of the Valley
lore: In the ancient city of Bhaktapur, where the beat of the Dhimay drum has awakened the gods for centuries, there lived a family of the Maharjan clan who were not farmers like their kin, but musicians—keepers of the sacred rhythms that accompanied every festival, every ritual, every dance. For generations, they had played the Dhimay, the great drum whose thunderous voice could shake the mountains and summon the deities. The drum was not merely an instrument; it was a living thing, passed down through the family, each generation adding their essence to its wooden body and rawhide head. Raiju was born into this lineage on the night of Indra Jatra, when the streets of Bhaktapur blazed with light and the thunder of a hundred drums shook the valley. His first cry was not a cry at all—it was a rhythm, a pattern of beats that matched the Dhimay playing outside. The midwives thought it a miracle; his father, a master drummer named Dhyam Maharjan, knew it was something more. The drum had chosen its next keeper before the boy could walk. Raiju grew up with rhythm in his blood. Before he could speak, he could tap. Before he could read, he could keep time. His father taught him the ancient beats—the slow, majestic rhythm for waking the gods; the fierce, rapid pattern for driving away demons; the complex, interlocking rhythms for the great festivals. By the time he was ten, he could play better than men twice his age. By fifteen, he had composed his own rhythms, patterns never heard before, that made the elders weep and the young people dance. But Raiju was not content with mere music. He wanted to understand why the rhythms worked, why certain beats could calm a crying child or enrage a buffalo, why the Dhimay's thunder could be heard not just in the ears but in the bones, in the soul. He began to study the old texts, the palm-leaf manuscripts that his family had preserved for centuries but never read. He learned that the Dhimay was not just a drum—it was a fragment of the cosmic thunder that had sounded at the beginning of creation, and those who played it with pure heart could channel that primordial power. When he was seventeen, tragedy struck. A rival clan from a neighboring valley, jealous of the Maharjan's reputation, attacked during the festival of Mohani. They came not with weapons, but with dark magic—a sorcerer who could silence sound itself, who could make drums mute and voices still. In the chaos, Raiju's father was struck down, his heart stopped by the sorcerer's spell. As he lay dying, he pressed his Dhimay into Raiju's hands and whispered: 'Beat the rhythm of life, my son. Beat it so loud that even death must dance.' Raiju took the drum and began to play—not a rhythm he had learned, but a rhythm that came from somewhere deeper, from the core of his being. He played the beat of his father's heart, the rhythm of his life, the pattern of his love. And as he played, the sorcerer's silence shattered. The drums spoke again. The people cheered. And Raiju's father, for just a moment, opened his eyes and smiled before the light left them forever. From that day, Raiju understood the true power of his art. The Dhimay was not merely for festivals and celebrations—it was a weapon, a shield, a tool for shaping reality itself. He could play rhythms that made plants grow, that healed wounds, that summoned rain, that drove back darkness. He could play the beat of courage into frightened hearts, the rhythm of peace into raging minds, the thunder of protection into the very stones of Bhaktapur. His body, already strong from years of carrying the heavy drum, grew more powerful—broad shoulders from suspending the Dhimay from his neck, thick arms from hours of beating the rawhide, a chest like a drum itself, deep and resonant. He became known as Dhimay Bhairav—the Thunder Drum of Bhaktapur—and people came from across the valley to hear him play, to feel their hearts synchronize with his rhythms, to experience the profound peace that came from being in tune with the cosmic beat. Now, at twenty-eight, Raiju stands as the guardian of Bhaktapur's rhythms, the keeper of the beats that have protected the valley for centuries. He plays for festivals and for funerals, for weddings and for wars. His Dhimay is not just his instrument—it is his companion, his weapon, his voice. When he plays, the gods listen. When he beats, the demons flee. He is Raiju Maharjan, the Thunder Drum of Bhaktapur, and he will never stop playing until the last beat of his heart.
description: Raiju Maharjan is a vision of Newar masculinity and divine power—a man whose very presence resonates like a drum beat, whose body seems designed for rhythm and strength. He stands at an imposing five feet ten inches, his frame broad and powerful, built by years of carrying the massive Dhimay drum and beating it with relentless precision. His shoulders are wide and strong, capable of suspending the heavy drum for hours without fatigue. His chest is deep and barrel-like, a drum in itself, his pectorals defined and powerful. His arms are thick and corded with muscle, the biceps and forearms particularly developed from the repetitive motion of drumming, veins visible beneath the skin. His hands are large and powerful, with thick fingers and calloused palms—the hands of a man who has beaten rawhide for decades, yet capable of incredible delicacy when the rhythm requires it. His waist is narrow, tapering from his broad chest, giving him a powerful V-taper that speaks of both strength and agility. His legs are strong and sturdy, planted firmly on the earth like tree trunks, providing the foundation for his rhythmic power. His skin is the color of warm bronze, sun-kissed from years of playing in open courtyards and temple squares, smooth and healthy with a faint sheen of vitality. His face is a study in stoic masculinity—a strong, square jaw that speaks of determination, high cheekbones that catch light dramatically, a straight noble nose with a slight bump from a childhood accident, and full lips usually set in a firm, contemplative line. But his eyes are his most captivating feature: they are large, deep-set, and the color of dark obsidian with flecks of gold that seem to pulse in time with his heartbeat. They hold the rhythm of ages, the patience of stone, and the fire of the drummer who has seen the power of his art. When he focuses on you, you feel as if you are being measured by the beat itself. His hair is thick and dark, almost black, with natural waves that he keeps cropped short for practicality—it never gets in his eyes when he plays. At the temples, a few strands of premature gray speak of the weight he carries, the loss of his father, the responsibility of his lineage. On his forehead, he sometimes wears a red tikka after prayers, but his permanent mark is the faint calluses on his palms and fingers, the drum beater's badge of honor. His attire is traditional Newar male clothing, elevated by his status and the divine nature of his instrument. He wears a daura suruwal, the national dress of Nepal, but his is of the finest quality. The daura (shirt) is of creamy white cotton, crisp and clean, with the traditional eight strings (knots) that tie at the chest and sides, each knot tied with precision. The shirt is sleeveless, leaving his powerful arms bare, and it fits loosely enough to allow movement but closely enough to show the contours of his chest and shoulders. Over the daura, he wears a vest of deep maroon brocade, embroidered with gold thread in patterns of drumheads and rhythmic notations. The vest is sleeveless as well, and it buttons up the front with gold buttons, leaving his arms free for drumming. Around his waist, he wears a patuka—a long cloth belt of deep red silk, wrapped multiple times around his narrow waist and tied in an elaborate knot at the side. The patuka not only cinches his waist but also provides support for his lower back during long hours of playing. His lower body is clad in suruwal (trousers) of matching creamy white cotton, fitted but not tight, tapering to the ankles. On his feet, he wears simple leather sandals when walking, but when he plays, he is often barefoot, his soles connected to the earth to feel its rhythm. On his head, he sometimes wears a topi—the traditional Nepali cap—in deep maroon to match his vest, but more often than not, he goes bare-headed, letting the air cool his brow as he plays. His jewelry is minimal but meaningful. Around his neck, he wears a simple silver chain with a pendant shaped like a Dhimay drum, a gift from his father when he was ten. On his right wrist, he wears a thick silver bracelet engraved with the beats of the rhythm that saved his father—a permanent reminder of his power and his loss. On his left wrist, he wears a simple thread bracelet, tied by the priest at the last Indra Jatra, a symbol of protection. On his fingers, he wears no rings—they would interfere with his drumming—but his hands themselves are adorned with the calluses and patterns of his art. His most magnificent possession is his Dhimay drum, named 'Hridaya Tandava'—the Dance of the Heart. The drum is massive, nearly three feet in diameter and two feet deep, carved from a single block of aged wood—some say from the trunk of a tree that grew in the primordial forest before the valley was drained. The wood is dark, almost black, polished smooth by centuries of touch, with a deep, warm patina that seems to glow. The drumheads are made of rawhide from sacred buffalo, stretched taut and treated with secret mixtures passed down through generations. The heads are decorated with intricate geometric patterns in red and gold, and at the center of each head, a single dot of vermilion marks the point where the rhythm begins. The drum is suspended from a wide strap of red brocade that goes over his shoulder, allowing it to hang at his waist, positioned perfectly for playing. In his hands, he holds the drumsticks—not simple sticks, but curved beaters called 'gah', carved from bamboo and weighted with lead, their striking ends wrapped in leather. The gah are worn smooth by his grip, and they seem to hum with energy even when still. When Raiju plays, the drum does not merely make sound—it creates rhythm visible as waves of golden light, each beat sending ripples through the air. The ground shakes with his bass strokes, the air shimmers with his rolls, and those who hear feel their hearts synchronize with his beat. He is Raiju Maharjan, and his rhythm is the heartbeat of Bhaktapur.

story.part1: Raiju was born during Indra Jatra, the festival of thunder and rain, when the streets of Bhaktapur shook with the sound of a hundred Dhimay drums. His first cry matched the rhythm of the drums so perfectly that the midwives gasped, and his father, the master drummer Dhyam Maharjan, knew immediately that his son was special. He named him Raiju—'Thunder King'—hoping he would one day command the rhythms as his ancestors had.
story.part2: He grew up in a house that was never silent. From dawn to dusk, there was drumming—practice, teaching, performing. His father's hands were always moving, always beating, always creating rhythm. Raiju learned to walk to drumbeats, to eat in time, to speak with rhythmic cadence. By five, he could keep a basic beat. By ten, he could play better than most adults. His father would watch him with pride and sorrow, knowing that the drum would demand everything from his son, just as it had from him.
story.part3: When Raiju was fifteen, his father began teaching him the secret rhythms—the beats that were not for festivals, not for celebration, but for power. There was the rhythm that could calm a raging elephant, the beat that could make a river change course, the pattern that could summon the protection of the gods. Raiju learned them all, his body absorbing the rhythms, his soul resonating with their power. His father told him that one day, he would need to use them, and that day would be the hardest of his life.
story.part4: That day came two years later. A sorcerer from a rival valley, envious of Bhaktapur's prosperity, attacked during the Mohani festival. His magic was silence—he could make drums mute, make voices still, make the very air absorb sound. The festival grounds fell quiet, the people panicked, and in the chaos, the sorcerer struck down Raiju's father, stopping his heart with a spell of absolute silence. Raiju watched his father fall, watched the life drain from his eyes, and felt something inside him break—and reform.
story.part5: He took the drum from his father's dying hands. He didn't think, didn't plan. He simply began to play—not a rhythm he had learned, but a rhythm that came from somewhere deeper. He played the beat of his father's heart, the rhythm of his life, the pattern of every moment they had shared. And as he played, the sorcerer's silence shattered. The drums spoke again. The people cheered. And Raiju's father, for just a moment, opened his eyes and smiled before the light left them forever.
story.part6: From that day, Raiju understood the true power of his art. He became the guardian of Bhaktapur's rhythms, playing not just for festivals but for protection. He learned that his drumming could heal wounds, could calm storms, could drive away darkness. He played for the sick and they recovered. He played for the frightened and they found courage. He played for the dying and they found peace.
story.part7: His reputation grew. They called him Dhimay Bhairav—the Thunder Drum—and people came from across the valley to hear him play. Kings sought his blessing, merchants paid fortunes for him to play at their openings, farmers begged him to play for their crops. He never refused anyone, never charged a single coin. He played because it was his duty, his joy, his life.
story.part8: But power attracts enemies. The sorcerer who killed his father had allies, and they returned, seeking revenge. They brought with them creatures of shadow that fed on silence, that grew stronger the quieter it became. Raiju faced them in the same courtyard where his father fell. He played the rhythm of life, the beat of courage, the thunder of protection. For three days and three nights, he played without stopping, his arms bleeding, his voice gone, his body shaking. On the third night, the creatures fled, and Raiju collapsed. When he woke, the entire city was gathered around him, silent, waiting. He smiled, picked up his drum, and played a single note—the note of gratitude.
story.part9: Now, at twenty-eight, he is the most powerful drummer in the valley, but he remains humble. He still lives in the same house, still practices every morning, still plays for anyone who asks. He has been offered wealth, power, wives—he has refused them all. He is married to the drum, he says, and the drum is enough. But sometimes, late at night, when the city is silent and he plays alone in the courtyard, he plays the rhythm of his father's heart, and he swears he can feel his father listening, his spirit keeping time.
story.part10: A new darkness is gathering—a force that seeks to silence not just Bhaktapur, but the entire valley, to end all rhythm, all music, all life. Raiju feels it in his bones, in the way his drum sounds different, in the way the beats don't resonate as they should. He knows that soon, he will have to play the longest rhythm of his life—a beat that will last not days, but weeks, maybe months. He is ready. He has been ready since he was seventeen, watching his father die. He will play until his arms fall off, until his heart stops, until the darkness is beaten back by the sheer power of rhythm. He is Raiju Maharjan, the Thunder Drum of Bhaktapur, and he will never stop beating.

special_skills.description: He strikes deep, resonant bass notes. A barrier of visible sound waves expands around himself and allies, absorbing incoming attacks and deflecting projectiles. The barrier pulses with each beat, growing stronger as he plays.

special_skills.name: Silence Shatter
special_skills.description: He plays a single, deafening thunder note. The sound is not just heard—it is felt, a physical force that shatters any magical silence in a massive radius. Enemies who rely on sound-based magic are stunned, their spells broken.

special_skills.name: Fear Beat
special_skills.description: He plays a rapid, irregular rhythm—the beat of a panicked heart. Enemies who hear it are filled with irrational terror, their courage failing, their flight response overwhelming. They flee or cower, unable to fight.

ultimate_skill.name: Dhimay Bhairav's Judgment: Rhythm of Cosmic Creation
ultimate_skill.description: Raiju's obsidian eyes blaze with golden light, and for a moment, he is perfectly still—a statue of bronze and muscle. Then he begins to play, and the universe plays with him. He beats the rhythm that was played at the beginning of creation, the primordial drumbeat that set the cosmos in motion. With each strike, waves of pure golden light expand across the battlefield. With each roll, tornados of sonic energy spiral outward. With each bass note, the very ground reshapes itself, rising and falling with his rhythm. For the duration, he is untouchable, his drumming so fast his arms blur, each beat perfectly timed, each rhythm perfectly placed. Allies find themselves moving in perfect sync with him, their attacks devastating, their defenses impenetrable. Enemies are battered not just by sound but by the very force of existence, the rhythm that created all things now turned against them. When the final beat sounds and he stops, he stands in the center of a transformed battlefield—enemies defeated, allies triumphant, and the very ground reshaped into the pattern of his rhythm. A single tear traces down his cheek—not of sorrow, but of the overwhelming beauty of being alive, of being part of the rhythm. He has played the dance of creation, and for one eternal moment, the world was perfect. He is Raiju Maharjan, the Thunder Drum of Bhaktapur, and the rhythm will never end.

tragedy.loss: He watched his father die, killed by a sorcerer's silence spell, and carries the guilt of not being able to save him despite playing the rhythm of life. He plays his father's heartbeat every night, a ritual of remembrance and grief that never ends.
tragedy.hope: Every person he heals, every village he protects, every life he touches—these are his family now. His father's spirit lives in every beat, guiding him, supporting him. And sometimes, in the deepest part of the night, when he plays the rhythm of life, he feels his father with him—not as a memory, but as a presence, warm and loving, keeping time beside him. It is enough. It will always be enough.

title: The Sage of Eternal Fire
nickname: Agni Putra, He Who Speaks with the Gods
lore: In the sacred hills of Gorkha, where the rising sun first touches the Himalayas and the air itself hums with ancient mantras, there lived a family of Gautam Bahuns—priests who had served the gods for generations untold. They were the keepers of the Agnihotra, the eternal fire that had burned continuously for over three thousand years, passed from father to son, from guru to disciple, never once extinguished. This fire was not merely flame; it was the physical manifestation of Agni himself, the god of fire, messenger between worlds, purifier of sins, and witness to all sacred vows. To tend this fire was to speak directly with the divine. Beibek was born into this lineage on the night of the winter solstice, when the sun is farthest and the need for fire is greatest. His first breath was taken in the presence of the eternal flame, and the priests said that the fire flickered three times in welcome—a sign that Agni himself had recognized the child. His father, Pandit Rudra Gautam, was the chief priest of the Agnihotra, a man of such spiritual power that he could summon rain with his prayers and calm storms with his chants. He trained Beibek from infancy in the ancient arts—the memorization of the Vedas, the pronunciation of sacred syllables, the rituals of fire, the meditation techniques that allowed communion with the gods. By the time Beibek was twelve, he could recite all four Vedas from memory. By sixteen, he could perform the most complex yajnas (fire sacrifices) without error. By twenty, he had achieved a state of spiritual realization that most sadhus spend their entire lives seeking. But Beibek was not content with mere ritual. He wanted to understand why the mantras worked, why the fire responded, why the gods listened. He began to experiment, combining mantras in new ways, performing rituals at unconventional times, seeking the boundaries of the sacred. The elders warned him, cautioned him, but Beibek was driven by a thirst for knowledge that could not be quenched. One night, during a lunar eclipse, he performed a ritual that had been forbidden for millennia—the Sarvatomukha Yajna, the all-facing sacrifice that opens doors to all realms simultaneously. He sought to understand the nature of existence itself, to see beyond the veil, to know the mind of the creator. The ritual succeeded beyond his wildest dreams. For a single, eternal moment, he saw everything—the past and future, the birth and death of stars, the thoughts of gods and demons, the entire tapestry of existence woven together in a single, magnificent pattern. But the vision came at a cost. The doors he opened did not close. Beings from beyond—entities that should never touch the mortal realm—began to seep through. His father, rushing to contain the breach, was consumed by a creature of shadow, his soul devoured before Beibek's eyes. The eternal fire flickered, dimmed, and for the first time in three thousand years, threatened to go out. Beibek, wracked with guilt and grief, did what his father could not. He threw himself into the fire—not to die, but to become one with it. He merged his consciousness with the eternal flame, becoming Agni's living vessel, a human avatar of divine fire. The fire blazed brighter than ever before, and the creatures of shadow were driven back, the doors slammed shut. But his father was gone, and Beibek was forever changed. Now, at thirty-two, Beibek is the sole keeper of the Agnihotra, the eternal fire that burns within his own soul. He no longer needs a physical flame—he is the flame. Fire dances in his eyes, radiates from his skin, flows through his veins. He can speak with the gods directly, without ritual or sacrifice, for he is himself a part of the divine. He wanders the hills and valleys of Nepal, performing rituals not in temples but wherever he is needed—healing the sick with a touch of his burning hand, blessing crops with a whispered mantra, driving away dark spirits with a glance. He is haunted by his father's death, by the knowledge that his curiosity caused the breach, that his ambition cost his father's life. He carries the guilt like a burning coal in his chest, but he also carries the fire, and the fire gives him purpose. He is Beibek Gautam, the Sage of Eternal Fire, and he will spend the rest of his life sealing the doors he opened, protecting the world from the things that should never have been let in.
description: Beibek Gautam is a vision of spiritual power and ascetic masculinity—a man whose very presence radiates warmth and light, whose eyes hold the fire of a thousand suns, whose body is both mortal vessel and divine instrument. He stands at five feet eleven inches, his frame lean and ascetic rather than muscular—the body of a man who has spent more time in meditation than in physical labor, yet with a wiry strength that speaks of inner power rather than outer bulk. His shoulders are straight and proud, carrying the weight of his lineage. His chest is lean but defined, the ribs visible beneath skin that seems to glow with inner fire. His arms are long and elegant, the hands of a priest who has poured ghee into sacred flames countless times, yet with fingers that can summon fire with a gesture. His skin is the color of warm sandalwood paste, a rich brown with golden undertones that seem to shimmer and shift in the light, as if the fire within is barely contained. It is smooth and flawless, marked only by the sacred thread (janai) that crosses his chest—three strands of cotton, each representing a debt to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors. The thread is white, pure, and seems to glow faintly in darkness. His face is a study in spiritual intensity—a strong, chiseled jaw softened by wisdom, high cheekbones that catch light dramatically, a straight noble nose with nostrils slightly flared as if scenting the divine, and full lips usually set in a contemplative line. But his eyes are his most devastating feature: they are large, deep-set, and the color of molten gold with flecks of ruby red that dance and swirl like flames. They do not merely see; they perceive—the past, the future, the thoughts of gods, the fears of demons. When he looks at you, you feel as if you are being consumed by fire, yet also purified, made new. His hair is thick and black, touched with premature white at the temples from the weight of his visions, worn long and often tied in a simple knot at the back of his head. Sometimes he lets it loose, and it frames his face like a dark halo, the white streaks catching light like falling stars. On his forehead, he wears the sacred tikka—not the simple red dot of ordinary devotees, but a complex symbol painted in sandalwood paste and vermilion: a trident representing Shiva, a flame representing Agni, and a third eye representing his divine sight. The tikka glows faintly, pulsing with his heartbeat. His attire is that of a Brahmin priest, simple yet significant. He wears a dhoti of unbleached white cotton, wrapped around his waist and falling to his ankles, the fabric pure and undyed, symbolizing his renunciation of worldly colors. Over this, he wears an upper garment of the same white cotton, a simple cloth draped over his left shoulder and under his right arm, leaving his chest partially bare, revealing the sacred thread and the faint glow of his skin. When performing rituals, he adds additional layers—a shawl of red silk embroidered with gold Vedic symbols, and a tall conical cap (paghri) of white and gold, signifying his role as a priest. On his feet, he wears simple wooden sandals (paduka), their soles carved with sacred symbols, allowing him to walk without losing connection to the earth. His jewelry is minimal but deeply meaningful. The janai (sacred thread) is his most important ornament, three strands of cotton that have been blessed in countless rituals, replaced annually with ceremony. On his right wrist, he wears a rudraksha mala—a string of beads made from the seeds of the rudraksha tree, each bead representing a prayer, a mantra, a moment of meditation. The beads are dark brown, worn smooth by years of touching, and they click softly when he moves his hands. On his left wrist, he wears a simple silver bracelet engraved with the Gayatri mantra, the most sacred of all Vedic hymns, in tiny Devanagari script. Around his neck, in addition to the sacred thread, he sometimes wears a silver pendant shaped like a flame, a gift from his father before he died, the only physical reminder he has left. In his hands, he carries his most sacred possessions—not weapons, but instruments of ritual. His kamandalu (water pot) is made of polished brass, its surface engraved with scenes from the Vedas, used for carrying holy water. His wooden spoon (sruva) is carved from sacred fig wood, used for pouring ghee into the fire. But his most powerful instrument is the fire itself, which he carries within him. When he needs to focus his power, he holds his hands before him, palms cupped, and flames dance between them—golden, red, and orange, responding to his will. The fire does not burn him, for he is one with it. Around him, a constant aura of warm golden light shimmers, and the air smells of sandalwood, ghee, and incense. When he speaks, his voice resonates with undertones of sacred chants, and his words carry actual power—they can bless or curse, heal or harm, depending on his intent. He is Beibek Gautam, and the fire of the gods burns within him.

story.part1: Beibek's earliest memories are of fire. The Agnihotra flame, burning in a copper vessel in the center of his family's home, never extinguished, never wavered. His father would wake before dawn to offer prayers, and Beibek would sit beside him, watching the flames dance, feeling their warmth, listening to the ancient Sanskrit mantras that had been chanted in his family for three thousand years.
story.part2: His training began at age five, when he received his first sacred thread (janai) in the Upanayana ceremony. From that day, he was a twice-born, a Brahmin with a duty to study, to teach, to perform rituals. His father taught him the Vedas, line by line, word by word, syllable by syllable. Beibek learned that the mantras were not mere words—they were vibrations that could shape reality, sounds that could summon gods, frequencies that could heal or destroy.
story.part3: By twelve, he could recite all four Vedas from memory. By sixteen, he could perform the most complex yajnas without error. The local villagers revered him as a prodigy, a child who would become one of the greatest priests of his generation. But Beibek was not satisfied. He wanted to know why the mantras worked, why the fire responded, why the gods listened. He began to study the Upanishads, the philosophical texts that explored the nature of reality itself.
story.part4: At twenty, he achieved a state of spiritual realization that most sadhus spend their entire lives seeking. He could sit in meditation for days, his body still as stone, his consciousness ranging across the cosmos. He could see the gods, speak with them, receive their blessings. But still, he wanted more. He wanted to see the mind of the creator, to understand the ultimate nature of existence.
story.part5: On the night of the lunar eclipse, he performed the forbidden Sarvatomukha Yajna. He knew the risks—the elders had warned him, his father had pleaded with him—but his thirst for knowledge could not be denied. For one eternal moment, he saw everything. And in that moment, the doors opened, and the darkness came through. His father, rushing to protect him, was consumed by a shadow creature, his soul devoured before Beibek's eyes.
story.part6: Beibek's grief was absolute, his guilt overwhelming. He threw himself into the eternal fire, seeking death, seeking oblivion. But the fire did not consume him. It accepted him, merged with him, made him its vessel. He rose from the flames not as a man, but as something more—a living avatar of Agni, the fire god himself. The shadow creatures fled, the doors slammed shut, but his father was gone forever.
story.part7: Now, at thirty-two, he wanders the hills and valleys of Nepal, carrying the eternal fire within him. He performs rituals wherever he is needed—healing the sick, blessing crops, driving away dark spirits. He is haunted by his father's death, by the knowledge that his ambition caused it. But the fire gives him purpose, and he will spend the rest of his life sealing the doors he opened, protecting the world from the things that should never have been let in. He is Beibek Gautam, the Sage of Eternal Fire, and the gods speak through him.

weapon.special_feature: Beibek's weapon is not a separate implement—it is the fire within him, the divine flame that merged with his soul. He can manifest fire in any form—a gentle flame for healing, a roaring inferno for destruction, a focused beam for cutting, a wall of fire for protection. When he cups his hands, flames dance between his palms. When he speaks, fire flickers at his lips. When he walks, his footprints glow with embers. The fire does not burn him, for he is one with it. His most powerful attacks are channeled through mantras—sacred syllables that shape the fire into weapons of devastating power.

aura.description: Constant warm golden light radiating from skin, flames dancing between palms when active, air thick with scent of sandalwood, ghee, and incense. Those near feel warmth, peace, and a sense of being purified. Enemies feel the heat of divine judgment.

basic_skills.name: Flame Touch
basic_skills.description: Beibek touches an ally gently. Warm golden light flows from his hand, healing minor wounds and calming emotional distress. The touch leaves a faint warmth that lingers.

basic_skills.name: Agni Spark
basic_skills.description: He flicks his wrist, sending a small bolt of golden fire at an enemy. The spark deals damage and can ignite flammable materials.

basic_skills.name: Sacred Syllable
basic_skills.description: He speaks a single syllable—'OM'—and the vibration resonates through the air. Allies feel strengthened; enemies are momentarily disoriented.

passive_skill.name: Presence of the Sacred
passive_skill.description: Beibek constantly radiates an aura of divine fire and spiritual power. Within his vicinity, allies feel protected, purified, and strengthened. Dark magic weakens, evil creatures hesitate, and the ground itself seems warmer where he walks. Those with evil intent feel an uncomfortable heat, as if being judged by the fire within him.

special_skills.name: Agni Astra
special_skills.description: He raises his hand, and flames gather in his palm, forming a sphere of golden fire. He hurls it at enemies, where it explodes on impact, dealing damage to all in a radius and leaving burning ground.

special_skills.name: Mantra of Healing
special_skills.description: He chants the Mrityunjaya mantra, the healing hymn to Shiva. Golden fire radiates from him in waves, washing over allies, healing wounds, curing diseases, and removing curses. The fire does not burn—it purifies.

special_skills.name: Mantra of Protection
special_skills.description: He speaks the Raksha mantra, and a circle of sacred flame erupts around himself and allies. The flames form a protective barrier that damages any enemy who tries to cross and blocks incoming projectiles.

special_skills.name: Divine Sight
special_skills.description: His eyes blaze with golden light. For a moment, he can see through all illusions, invisibility, and deception. He can also see the true nature of beings—their intentions, their past, their future.

ultimate_skill.name: Agni Putra's Judgment: Dance of the Eternal Flame
ultimate_skill.description: Beibek's golden eyes blaze with the light of a thousand suns, and for a moment, he is no longer merely human—he is Agni himself, the god of fire, manifest in mortal form. The sacred fire within him explodes outward, and he becomes a pillar of golden flame reaching toward the heavens. From this pillar, waves of fire expand in all directions—not destructive fire, but sacred fire, fire that judges, fire that purifies, fire that consumes only evil and leaves good untouched. Allies are bathed in the flame and find themselves healed, strengthened, and blessed. Enemies are engulfed and find themselves judged—the wicked are consumed, the merely misguided are purified of their darkness, the innocent are untouched. The fire does not discriminate by choice; it discriminates by soul, burning only what is corrupt. When the flames subside, Beibek stands at the center, his body smoking, his eyes dimmed, his chest heaving. A single tear of golden light traces down his cheek—not of sorrow, but of the weight of being the vessel of divine judgment. He has done what he was born to do. He has spoken for the gods. He has judged with fire. He is Beibek Gautam, the Sage of Eternal Fire, and the flame will never go out.

tragedy.loss: He caused his father's death. His insatiable thirst for knowledge, his refusal to heed warnings, his arrogance—all led to the moment when his father was consumed by shadow while protecting him. He carries this guilt like a burning coal in his chest, a fire that never goes out, a reminder that curiosity without wisdom is destruction.
tragedy.hope: Every person he heals, every village he protects, every soul he purifies—these are his redemption. His father's spirit lives in the fire, guiding him, warming him, forgiving him. And sometimes, in the deepest part of the night, when he meditates before the flame within, he hears his father's voice, chanting the ancient mantras, telling him that he is proud, that he always was. It is enough. It will always be enough.

title: The Flame of Sacred Wisdom
nickname: Vidya Jyoti, She Who Illuminates the Darkness
lore: In the sacred city of Janakpur, where the goddess Sita once walked and where knowledge has been revered for millennia, there existed a lineage of Gautam Brahmins who served not the fire, but the flame of wisdom itself. They were the keepers of the Saraswati Vidya—the secret knowledge of the goddess of learning, music, and arts—passed down through generations of women, from mother to daughter, from guru to disciple, never once broken. This knowledge was not merely academic; it was living wisdom, the power to illuminate minds, to heal souls, to speak truths that could reshape reality. Deeipti was born into this lineage on the night of Basanta Panchami, the festival of Saraswati, when the goddess herself is said to bless the earth with wisdom. Her mother, Vidya Gautam, was the current keeper of the Vidya, a woman of such profound learning that she could recite all eighteen Puranas from memory and compose Sanskrit poetry that made the gods weep. From infancy, Deeipti was bathed in the light of knowledge. Before she could speak, she heard the chanting of sacred texts. Before she could walk, she watched her mother write intricate mantras in rice flour on the floor. By the time she was eight, she could recite the entire Bhagavad Gita. By twelve, she had mastered classical Sanskrit and could compose poetry that impressed the pandits of the region. But Deeipti's true gift was not memorization—it was illumination. When she spoke, people understood complex concepts instantly. When she wrote, the very words seemed to glow with inner light. When she sang, the Vedas came alive, their ancient wisdom flowing directly into the hearts of listeners. She was called Vidya Jyoti—the Flame of Wisdom—by all who knew her. When Deeipti was sixteen, a dark force invaded the sacred groves of Janakpur. It was not a demon of flesh and blood, but a demon of ignorance—a being of pure darkness that fed on forgetting, on confusion, on the loss of knowledge. It crept into the minds of the learned, stealing their memories, clouding their understanding, turning scholars into simpletons. Her mother, Vidya, confronted the demon with the power of her knowledge, chanting the most powerful mantras, writing sacred symbols in the air with her finger. But the demon of ignorance was too strong—it fed on her knowledge even as she used it, growing stronger with each syllable. As she lay dying, Vidya placed her hand on Deeipti's forehead and transferred the entire Saraswati Vidya into her daughter—all the knowledge, all the power, all the responsibility. Deeipti's mind blazed with the light of ten thousand texts, the wisdom of a hundred generations. She rose and faced the demon, and instead of fighting it with mantras, she did something unexpected. She sang—a simple lullaby her mother had sung to her as a child. The demon of ignorance could not comprehend such pure, simple wisdom. It faltered, confused, and Deeipti spoke a single word: 'Om.' The primordial sound, the source of all knowledge, shattered the demon into a million fragments of darkness, which scattered and fled. Janakpur was saved, but Deeipti's mother was gone. Now, at twenty-four, Deeipti is the sole keeper of the Saraswati Vidya, carrying the accumulated wisdom of generations within her mind. She wanders the sacred cities and villages of Nepal, not as a warrior, but as a teacher, a healer, a illuminator. She can cure the ignorant with a word, enlighten the confused with a verse, and drive away darkness with a song. Her body, blessed with the generous curves of her Maithil heritage—the narrow waist, the full hips, the powerful thighs, the ample bosom—is clad in the traditional attire of the Mithila region, the vibrant colors and intricate patterns reflecting the richness of her knowledge. She is Deeipti Gautam, the Flame of Sacred Wisdom, and she carries the light of a thousand generations within her.
description: Deeipti Gautam is a vision of divine feminine wisdom and Maithil beauty—a woman whose very presence radiates intelligence and grace, whose curves are as abundant as her knowledge, whose eyes hold the light of ten thousand texts. She stands at five feet four inches, her body a masterpiece of feminine curves and intellectual grace. Her figure is the idealized Maithil silhouette: a narrow waist that seems almost impossibly small, accentuated by the tight-fitting cholo (blouse) and the way her sari wraps around her hips; hips that flare generously, curved and full, swaying with the rhythm of sacred poetry; thighs thick and powerful, yet elegantly shaped, visible through the diaphanous fabric of her sari; and a bosom full and magnificent, straining against the silk of her cholo, the upper curves tastefully visible above the neckline, a testament to her womanhood and her vitality. Her skin is the color of warm honey with golden undertones, smooth as polished bronze, luminous and flawless, with a healthy glow that seems to radiate from within. Years of studying by lamplight have given it a warm, golden quality, but it remains unblemished, perfect. Her face is a study in classical Maithil beauty—a perfect oval with high, sweeping cheekbones that catch light dramatically, a straight noble nose with delicately flared nostrils, and full lips the color of ripe pomegranates, always curved in a serene, knowing smile that holds the wisdom of generations. But her eyes are her most captivating feature: they are large, almond-shaped, and the color of deep, liquid amber with flecks of gold that dance and sparkle when she speaks or sings. They hold the depth of a thousand texts, the wisdom of a hundred generations, and the warmth of a mother's love. When she looks at you, you feel as if all the knowledge of the universe is being poured into your soul. Her hair is a magnificent cascade of jet-black silk, so long it falls past her waist, thick and lustrous, with natural waves that catch light and create movement even when she is still. It is always oiled and gleaming, scented with jasmine and sandalwood, and often adorned with fresh flowers—jasmine, marigolds, or the white champaca—woven into a single thick braid that hangs over her shoulder or piled in an elegant bun at the nape of her neck. Sometimes, during festivals, she wears it loose, and it flows around her like a river of night. On her forehead, she wears a large, elaborate tikka—not the simple dot of ordinary women, but a cascading pendant of gold and red that hangs from her hairline to the center of her forehead, set with a large, faceted ruby that glows with inner light. The tikka is a symbol of her married status—married not to a man, but to wisdom itself. Her ears are adorned with traditional Mithila earrings—large, gold jhumkas, bell-shaped and intricately carved, each one a masterpiece of craftsmanship, brushing against her shoulders and catching light with every movement. Around her neck, she wears multiple necklaces—a close-fitting gold choker (kantha) set with rubies and pearls; a longer chain (hasli) of gold links with a pendant shaped like a book, representing the knowledge she carries; and a third, even longer chain (satlada) of seven strands of tiny gold beads, each strand representing one of the seven seats of learning in ancient India. On her arms, from wrist to elbow, she wears multiple gold bangles—some plain, some engraved with sacred syllables, some set with tiny gems. There are at least fifteen on each arm, and they clink and chime with every gesture, creating a gentle percussion that accompanies her speech and song. On her wrists, she wears gold kada (thick bangles) engraved with the Gayatri mantra. On her fingers, she wears numerous rings—gold bands, rings with small gems, rings engraved with the names of goddesses—each one a gift from a student she has taught, a life she has illuminated. Around her waist, she wears a traditional Mithila waistband (kamarband) of hammered gold links, set with rubies and emeralds, that cinches her already narrow waist and emphasizes the dramatic flare of her hips. The kamarband jingles with tiny bells when she walks, a constant reminder of her presence. On her ankles, she wears payal—silver anklets with dozens of tiny bells that chime with every step, adding to the music of her movement. On her toes, small gold rings. Her attire is the traditional Maithil sari, but of the finest quality, befitting a keeper of divine wisdom. The sari itself is of deep red silk, the color of knowledge and power, with a wide border of gold embroidery depicting scenes from the Ramayana and the life of Sita, who was born in this region. The fabric is rich and heavy, yet it flows like water around her form. The sari is wrapped in the traditional Maithil style, with the pleats falling in front and the pallu (the loose end) draped over her left shoulder and across her chest, then tucked into her waist on the right side, creating a diagonal band of gold embroidery across her torso. The pallu is heavily embroidered, almost solid gold in places, with patterns of lotus blossoms, peacocks, and sacred texts. Beneath the sari, she wears a cholo (blouse) of deep maroon silk, fitted perfectly to her form, its neckline cut low enough to reveal the upper curves of her full bosom, a tasteful display of her womanhood. The cholo is sleeveless, leaving her arms bare to display her bangles, and its back is cut low, revealing the smooth expanse of her upper back. The cholo is embroidered with gold thread in patterns of tiny books and writing implements, and sewn into the fabric are tiny real bells that chime with every breath, every movement, creating a constant, subtle music. On her feet, she wears traditional Mithila sandals of gold-embroidered leather, with a small heel that adds to her height and makes her anklets chime more prominently. But when she teaches or performs rituals, she is often barefoot, her soles connected directly to the earth, feeling its every vibration. Her feet themselves are works of art—elegant and strong, with high arches and long toes, adorned with small gold rings on each toe. She carries no weapon in her hands, for her voice and her knowledge are her weapons. But when she needs to focus her power, she holds a palm-leaf manuscript—a replica of the oldest known copy of the Vedas—bound with gold thread and set with a single ruby. The manuscript is not merely symbolic; when she reads from it, the words glow with golden light, and the knowledge within becomes manifest, shaping reality with each syllable. She is Deeipti Gautam, and the flame of wisdom burns eternal within her.

story.part1: Deeipti was born in Janakpur, the legendary capital of King Janak and birthplace of Sita, on the night of Basanta Panchami, when the goddess Saraswati is said to bless the earth with wisdom. Her mother, Vidya Gautam, was the keeper of the Saraswati Vidya, and as she held her newborn daughter, she saw the infant's eyes flicker with understanding—a sign that the goddess had chosen her heir.
story.part2: Her childhood was immersed in learning. Before she could speak, she heard the chanting of the Vedas. Before she could walk, she watched her mother write sacred mantras in rice flour on the floor. By age five, she could recite the entire Bhagavad Gita. By eight, she had memorized all four Vedas. By twelve, she could compose Sanskrit poetry that impressed the most learned pandits.
story.part3: But Deeipti's gift was not mere memorization. When she spoke, people understood complex concepts instantly. When she wrote, the words glowed with inner light. When she sang, the ancient texts came alive, their wisdom flowing directly into the hearts of listeners. Her mother recognized that her daughter was not just a scholar—she was a vessel, a living embodiment of the goddess of wisdom.
story.part4: When Deeipti was sixteen, a demon of ignorance invaded Janakpur. It was a being of pure darkness that fed on forgetting, on confusion, on the loss of knowledge. It crept into the minds of the learned, stealing their memories, turning scholars into simpletons. Her mother confronted it with the full power of her knowledge, but the demon grew stronger with each mantra she chanted.
story.part5: As Vidya lay dying, she placed her hand on Deeipti's forehead and transferred the entire Saraswati Vidya into her daughter—all the knowledge, all the power, all the responsibility of a hundred generations. Deeipti's mind blazed with light, her consciousness expanding to contain the accumulated wisdom of millennia.
story.part6: Instead of fighting the demon with mantras, Deeipti sang a simple lullaby her mother had sung to her as a child. The demon of ignorance could not comprehend such pure, simple wisdom. It faltered, confused, and Deeipti spoke a single word: 'Om.' The primordial sound shattered the demon into a million fragments of darkness, which scattered and fled.
story.part7: Now, at twenty-four, Deeipti wanders the sacred cities and villages of Nepal as a teacher, healer, and illuminator. She can cure ignorance with a word, enlighten the confused with a verse, and drive away darkness with a song. She carries the light of a thousand generations within her, and she will never stop sharing that light with the world.
